title: Music is universal
description: A 2019 Harvard-led study found music in every one of 315 societies it examined, with lullabies and dance songs everywhere.

facts.text: A Harvard-led study published in Science in 2019 examined ethnographic records of 315 societies and found music in every one of them.
The same 2019 study found that lullabies and dance songs are ubiquitous across the world's societies.

title: Rhythm, melody and harmony
description: Music combines sounds, usually by cultural standards of rhythm (when), melody (which notes in a line) and, in most Western music, harmony (notes at once).

facts.text: Britannica defines music as combining sounds for beauty of form or emotional expression, usually by cultural standards of rhythm, melody and, in most Western music, harmony.
Rhythm is the organization of sounds in time: patterns of long and short sounds over a steady beat.
A melody is a sequence of single notes heard as one coherent line, often the most recognizable part of a piece of music.
Harmony is the sound of two or more notes heard at the same time; notes sounding together form chords, and a three-note chord is called a triad.

title: Sound is vibration
description: Sound is a pressure wave: a vibrating object pushes air into compressions and rarefactions that pass outward through a medium, and cannot cross a vacuum.

facts.text: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium such as air, water or a solid; it cannot travel through a vacuum.
A vibrating object pushes on the air, making compressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure) that travel outward as a pressure wave.
In a sound wave, air molecules oscillate back and forth along the wave's direction instead of traveling along with it, like a squeeze running down a coiled spring.
The eardrum vibrates from incoming sound waves and passes the vibrations to three tiny bones in the middle ear.

title: The speed of sound
description: Sound crosses about 343 meters of air per second at 20 C, far slower than light, so thunder lags lightning by about 3 seconds per kilometer.

facts.text: Sound travels through air at about 343 meters per second at 20 C.
Light arrives almost at once but sound covers about a kilometer every 3 seconds, so each 3 seconds from lightning to thunder means about 1 km.

title: Pitch is frequency
description: How high or low a note sounds (pitch) is how we hear frequency, the number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.

facts.text: Pitch is how we perceive frequency: a sound is higher or lower according to how many times per second its source vibrates, measured in hertz (Hz).

title: A = 440 Hz
description: The international tuning standard sets the A above middle C at 440 Hz: agreed in 1939 and confirmed as ISO 16 in 1975, after decades of local pitches.

facts.text: The international standard tuning pitch sets the A above middle C at 440 Hz; it was agreed in 1939 and confirmed as ISO 16 in 1975.
Before 1939 the tuning A varied by place: France's diapason normal set it at 435 Hz, while Britain's Old Philharmonic Pitch was above 450 Hz.

title: The range of hearing
description: Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and with age most people lose the highest pitches first.

facts.text: Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).
Age-related hearing loss most often affects high-pitched sounds, like a phone ringing or a microwave beeping, while low-pitched hearing is often unaffected.

title: Beat and tempo
description: The beat is music's steady pulse; tempo is how fast it goes, counted in beats per minute or named with Italian terms like adagio and allegro.

facts.text: The beat is the steady pulse listeners perceive in music, the regular unit that divides musical time.
Tempo is the speed of the beat, often counted in beats per minute (BPM); at 60 BPM one beat falls every second, and 120 BPM is twice as fast.
Traditional Italian tempo markings include adagio (slow), andante (at a walking pace), allegro (fast) and presto (very fast).

title: Meter
description: Meter groups beats into regular measures of strong and weak beats, usually in twos or threes; a waltz counts in threes (3/4 time).

facts.text: Meter organizes beats into regular groups called measures or bars; listeners tend to hear beats in groups of two or three, with strong and weak beats.
The waltz is danced in 3/4 time, three beats to a measure.

title: Melodic contour
description: A melody has a contour, the shape it traces as it rises, falls or arches, moving by steps or by leaps.

facts.text: A melody's contour is its overall shape as it rises, falls or arches; melodies move by steps to neighboring notes or by leaps over several.

title: A melody is a pattern
description: People recognize a melody by the relationships between its notes, so it survives new words and a new starting note: one tune carries Twinkle, the alphabet song and Baa, Baa, Black Sheep.

facts.text: The melody of the French song "Ah, vous dirai-je, Maman", first published without words in 1761 by an unknown composer, carries Twinkle, Twinkle, the alphabet song and Baa, Baa, Black Sheep.
Contour and intervals depend on the relationships between notes, not their exact pitches, so most people recognize a melody moved to a new starting note (transposed).

title: Chords and triads
description: A triad stacks three notes, a root, a third and a fifth; C-E-G is the C major triad.

facts.text: A triad is a chord of three notes, the root, third and fifth; traditional Western harmony builds chords by stacking thirds, as in C-E-G, the C major triad.

title: Consonance and dissonance
description: Consonant combinations sound stable, dissonant ones tense; music moves between them, and the preference for consonance depends heavily on what music you know.

facts.text: Consonance gives an impression of stability and rest; dissonance creates tension or clash; music uses both to build and release tension.
Traditional Western theory counts seconds (like two neighboring keys) and sevenths as dissonant, and octaves, fifths, thirds and sixths as consonant.
In a 2016 study, the Tsimane' of the Bolivian Amazon, with little exposure to Western music, told consonant and dissonant chords apart but rated them equally pleasant.
The 2016 study concluded that preferring consonance depends on exposure to Western music and is not innate; American listeners, especially musicians, preferred it most.

title: Major and minor chords
description: Major and minor triads share a root and a fifth; the minor third is one semitone lower (three semitones above the root instead of four).

facts.text: A semitone (half step) is the smallest step on a keyboard, from one key to the very next, black or white; two semitones make a tone.
A major triad has a major third (four semitones) above its root; a minor triad has a minor third (three semitones); both have a perfect fifth: C-E-G vs C-E flat-G.

title: Is minor sad?
description: Hearing major as happy and minor as sad is largely learned: children pick it up around age 6, and it is weak where Western music is unfamiliar.

facts.text: In a 2001 study, 3- and 4-year-olds did not reliably tell happy from sad music; 5-year-olds judged by tempo alone; 6- to 8-year-olds, like adults, used tempo and major/minor.
A 2022 study of 170 people in Papua New Guinea found that hearing major as happier than minor was strongly tied to exposure to Western-style music such as church hymns.
The 2022 study's authors said they could not exclude a small universal effect, but the pattern points mainly to culture.

title: The octave
description: An octave up doubles the frequency (A 440 Hz to 880 Hz); notes an octave apart sound like the same note and share a letter name.

facts.text: An octave is the interval whose higher note vibrates twice as fast as the lower: above the 440 Hz A is an A at 880 Hz, and below it one at 220 Hz.
Notes an octave apart are heard as the same note at a different height, and they share a letter name: after G the letters start again at A.
The octave is a constant in the scales of most of the world's musical cultures.

title: Scales
description: A scale picks notes inside the octave. Western music splits it into 12 semitones and the major scale follows tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone; other traditions use other ladders.

facts.text: A scale is a graduated sequence of notes dividing the octave; what defines it is its pattern of intervals.
Equal temperament, the standard tuning of Western keyboards, divides the octave into 12 equal semitones.
The major scale follows tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone; started on C it gives C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C, the white keys.
Five-note pentatonic scales are found, in different forms, in most of the world's music, including Native American, sub-Saharan African and East Asian traditions and European folk songs.
Many traditions, including Arabic and Indian classical music, use intervals smaller than a semitone, notes that fall between a piano's keys.

title: The staff and clefs
description: Music is written on a five-line staff that works like a graph (up is higher, left to right is time); a clef names the lines.

facts.text: The five-line staff works like graph paper: the higher a note sits, the higher its pitch, and music reads left to right in time, divided by bar lines.
A staff has five lines and four spaces; notes sit on the lines and in the spaces, each position one letter step from the next.
The treble clef, a curly G, marks the second line from the bottom as the G above middle C, so its lines read E, G, B, D, F and its spaces F, A, C, E.
The bass clef, a stylized F, marks the second line from the top as F.
Stacking a treble staff over a bass staff makes the grand staff; middle C sits on its own short line between them.

title: Note values
description: A note's shape gives its length: each value lasts half as long as the one above, so a whole note equals two halves or four quarters.

facts.text: Each note value lasts half as long as the one above it: a whole note lasts as long as two half notes or four quarter notes.
A whole note is an open oval with no stem; a half note is open with a stem; a quarter note has a filled-in head and a stem.

title: The ear sorts pitch
description: Inside the cochlea, hair cells near the wide end respond to high pitches and those toward the center to low pitches, so each pitch has its own place.

facts.text: Hair cells near the wide end of the snail-shaped cochlea detect higher-pitched sounds, like an infant crying; those closer to the center detect lower ones, like a large dog barking.

title: Sorting instruments by what vibrates
description: The Hornbostel-Sachs system (1914) sorts instruments by what vibrates first: idiophones, membranophones, chordophones and aerophones.

facts.text: In 1914 Erich von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs published a system that sorts musical instruments by what vibrates to make the sound, not by material or origin.
Its four classes: idiophones (the instrument's own body vibrates, as in bells and rattles), membranophones (a stretched membrane, as in drums), chordophones (strings) and aerophones (air).
A piano's wire strings sound when struck by felt-covered hammers operated from a keyboard.

title: The orchestra's four sections
description: An orchestra groups instruments into strings, woodwinds, brass and percussion; woodwinds and brass are both aerophones, and percussion gathers idiophones and membranophones.

facts.text: The modern symphony orchestra is arranged in four sections: strings, woodwinds, brass and percussion.
Percussion instruments are idiophones or membranophones; most are struck, but some are shaken, scraped, rubbed or plucked.

title: How a string sets its note
description: A shorter, tighter or lighter string sounds higher; halving the length raises the note an octave.

facts.text: A string sounds higher when it is shorter, tighter or lighter, and lower when it is longer, looser or heavier (thicker).
Halving a string's vibrating length doubles its frequency, raising its note an octave.

title: Bows and bodies
description: A bow keeps a string vibrating by stick-slip; the string barely moves air, so the bridge drives the body, which makes the sound. The violin family: violin, viola, cello, double bass.

facts.text: Strings alone make hardly any sound because they are thin and slip through the air; the bridge passes their vibration to the body, which moves the air.
A rosined bow grips the string and drags it sideways until the string slips back; this stick-slip cycle repeats once per vibration, keeping the note going.
The violin is the smallest, highest-pitched member of the violin family, which also includes the viola, the cello and the double bass.

title: The air column and tone holes
description: In a woodwind the air column vibrates; opening tone holes acts like shortening the pipe and raises the note.

facts.text: A woodwind's note depends on the length of its vibrating air column; opening tone holes from the far end acts like shortening the pipe, raising the pitch.

title: Edges and reeds
description: Woodwinds start the air vibrating with an edge (flutes), a single reed (clarinet, saxophone) or a double reed (oboe, bassoon); the metal saxophone is a woodwind because of its reed.

facts.text: Woodwinds start their air vibrating three ways: a flute's air stream against an edge, a single reed (clarinet, saxophone) or a double reed (oboe, bassoon).
A clarinet's reed works like a fast-opening and closing valve on the air flowing into the tube.
Woodwinds were traditionally made of wood but may now be metal; the family is set by how the sound starts, and the metal saxophone counts as a woodwind.
Antoine-Joseph (Adolphe) Sax patented the saxophone in Paris in 1846: a metal tube, originally brass, with a single-reed mouthpiece like a clarinet's.

title: Buzzing lips and the harmonic series
description: Brass players buzz their lips into a cup mouthpiece; lip tension picks notes from the tube's harmonic series, whole-number multiples of the fundamental.

facts.text: Brass instruments are sounded by the player's lips vibrating against a cup- or funnel-shaped mouthpiece, which sets the air column vibrating.
Tighter lips spring back faster, so high lip tension gives a high frequency and a high pitch.
The harmonic series is the set of frequencies at whole-number multiples of a fundamental: two times, three times, four times and so on.
Without valves or a slide, a brass tube plays only its harmonic series, and the player picks among those notes with lips and breath; the bugle works this way.

title: Valves and slides
description: Valves (about 1815) add tubing to lower the note and fill the gaps between harmonics; the trombone uses a slide.

facts.text: Valves, invented about 1815, send the air through extra tubing when pressed; the longer tube gives a lower set of notes, filling in the gaps.
On a trumpet, the first valve lowers the pitch by a tone, the second by a semitone and the third by three semitones.
The trombone uses a slide instead of valves, changing its tube length continuously.

title: Pitched and unpitched percussion
description: Some percussion (xylophones, timpani) plays definite pitches; some (cymbals, snare drums) has none; the family mostly marks rhythm.

facts.text: Some percussion, such as xylophones and timpani, sounds definite pitches; others, such as cymbals and snare drums, have no definite pitch.
Many percussion instruments can play melody, but they typically serve to mark or emphasize rhythm.

title: Tuning a drum
description: A tighter drumhead sounds higher; timpani use this to play definite notes, usually in pairs.

facts.text: The tighter a drum's membrane is stretched, the higher its pitch.
Timpani are the only Western orchestral drums tuned to definite pitch; they are usually played in pairs tuned to different pitches.
By the 16th century, screws around the copper shells of kettledrums were used to tighten and tune their heads.

title: Cristofori's soft-loud keyboard
description: Around 1700 in Florence, Cristofori replaced the harpsichord's plucking with hammers, making a keyboard that plays soft or loud by touch: the pianoforte.

facts.text: Bartolomeo Cristofori worked at the Medici court in Florence, where he cared for its harpsichords and other instruments.
By about 1700 Cristofori had built a keyboard he called a harpsichord with soft and loud (gravicembalo col piano e forte), the source of the name pianoforte, or piano.
A harpsichord plucks its strings with small quill or leather plectra, and the player cannot make a note louder or softer by pressing harder.
A piano Cristofori built in 1720, now at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, is the oldest surviving piano.

title: Hammers, escapement and dampers
description: Piano hammers strike the strings harder when you press harder; the escapement lets them fall away at once; dampers stop the strings, and the right pedal lifts them.

facts.text: On a piano, pressing a key harder makes the hammer strike harder, so the note sounds louder: it plays soft or loud by the fingers' pressure.
Cristofori's escapement lets the hammer fall away from the string the instant after it strikes, so it does not damp the sound.
Felt dampers stop a piano's strings when a key is released; the right pedal lifts all the dampers so every string can vibrate freely.

title: How a guitar works
description: Frets shorten the vibrating string to change notes; the bridge passes the vibration to the top plate, which makes the sound.

facts.text: Frets are note markers across a fingerboard; pressing a string against one shortens its vibrating length, giving a different pitch.
On an acoustic guitar, the strings barely sound on their own; the bridge and saddle pass their vibration to the top plate, which radiates the sound.

title: The guitar's family tree
description: The guitar grew from a four-course Spanish instrument to six strings and Torres's classical guitar, and spread into relatives like the jarana, the charango and the ukulele.

facts.text: The guitar probably originated in Spain early in the 16th century, with four courses (sets) of strings.
A fifth course of strings was added before 1600 and a sixth by the late 18th century; single strings tuned E-A-D-G-B-E became the standard.
In the 19th century the Spanish maker Antonio de Torres gave the classical guitar its modern form.
Latin America has its own small guitars, such as the Mexican jarana and the South American charango.
The ukulele comes from the machete, a small four-string guitar brought to Hawaii by Portuguese immigrants in the 1870s; its Hawaiian name means flea.

title: Pipes, ranks and stops
description: An organ blows pressurized air into pipes, one pipe per key in each rank; flue pipes sound by an air jet, reed pipes by a reed; stops bring ranks into play.

facts.text: An organ sends pressurized air from bellows or a blower into pipes; a basic organ has one rank of pipes, one pipe for each key.
Most organs have several ranks, called stops; the player draws a stop to bring its rank into play.
In an organ's flue pipes a jet of air vibrates against an edge; in its reed pipes a metal reed vibrates.

title: Pipe length and pitch
description: Doubling an organ pipe's length drops its note an octave (8-foot normal pitch, 16-foot an octave down); pipes span 32 feet to under an inch, down to about 16 Hz.

facts.text: An 8-foot organ pipe sounds at normal keyboard pitch; a 16-foot pipe sounds an octave lower and a 4-foot pipe an octave higher.
Organ pipes range from 32 feet long to less than an inch, giving the organ a possible range of nine octaves.
Large pipe organs can sound notes as low as about 16 Hz.

title: How the voice makes sound
description: Air from the lungs vibrates the vocal folds; their tension sets the pitch, and the throat, nose and mouth shape the sound.

facts.text: The voice starts when air from the lungs passes through the larynx and makes the two vocal folds vibrate.
Changing the tension of the vocal folds changes the voice's pitch, much like tuning a guitar string.
The throat, nose and mouth act as resonating spaces that shape the sound of the voice.

title: Voice types
description: Four-part music uses soprano, alto, tenor and bass, with baritone between tenor and bass; men's ranges are typically about an octave below women's.

facts.text: In four-part music, soprano is the highest voice and alto (contralto) the second-highest; tenor is the higher male voice and bass the lowest.
Baritone, the most common male voice, lies between tenor and bass.
Men's singing ranges are typically about an octave lower than women's.

title: Timbre
description: Timbre (tone color) comes from which harmonics sound with the fundamental and how strong they are, so the same pitch sounds different on each instrument.

facts.text: Timbre, or tone color, is what makes two instruments sound different on the same pitch at the same loudness; it depends on which harmonics are present and how strong they are.
Instruments sound a fundamental plus harmonics; flutes and violins produce all the harmonics, while clarinets emphasize the odd ones.
A tuning fork sounds clear and pure because it produces almost no overtones.

title: The oldest accepted instruments
description: Bone and ivory flutes from caves in southwestern Germany, over 35,000 years old at Hohle Fels and 42,000 to 43,000 at Geissenklösterle, made by early modern humans.

facts.text: The Hohle Fels flute, from a cave in southwestern Germany, was pieced together from 12 fragments of a griffon vulture's radius, a wing bone, and has five finger holes.
The surviving Hohle Fels flute is 21.8 cm long.
The Hohle Fels flutes are more than 35,000 years old; Nature published them in 2009 as evidence of an established musical tradition among Europe's first modern humans.

Flutes of bird bone and mammoth ivory from Geissenklösterle Cave in southern Germany were dated in 2012, by Oxford and Tübingen scientists using animal bones from the same layers, to 42,000 to 43,000 years old.
The researchers concluded that the first modern humans in Europe were already playing musical instruments about 40,000 years ago.

title: The Divje Babe debate
description: A holed cave bear bone from Slovenia, claimed as a Neanderthal flute, that many scientists think was chewed by hyenas.

facts.text: In 1995 a juvenile cave bear's thigh bone with round holes was found in Divje Babe cave in Slovenia; it is more than 40,000 years old.
Its finders argued that Neanderthals made the holes, and the National Museum of Slovenia still presents it as a Neanderthal flute.
In 2015 a paleobiologist reported marks of Ice Age hyena teeth at the holes, and most paleoanthropologists accept it as a bone chewed by carnivores.

title: Pythagoras and musical ratios
description: Greek tradition credits Pythagoras with linking the octave, fifth and fourth to string-length ratios 2:1, 3:2 and 4:3; the hammer story is a legend.

facts.text: Greek tradition credits Pythagoras, a 6th-century-BCE philosopher, with finding that the octave, fifth and fourth match the ratios 2:1, 3:2 and 4:3, seen in string lengths.
At the same tension, a string half as long vibrates twice as fast, so the 2:1 length ratio sounds an octave higher.
The story that Pythagoras heard the ratios in a blacksmith's hammers is false: a hammer's pitch is not simply proportional to its weight.
Pythagoras may have known the ratios without discovering them; the first workable experiment is credited to Hippasus, a Pythagorean active after his death.

title: Music in Greek life and thought
description: Mousike, the art of the Muses; Plato and Aristotle's belief that music shapes the soul; music and chorus at the heart of Greek drama.

facts.text: The word music comes, through Latin, from the Greek mousike, the art of the Muses.
Plato and Aristotle held that music acts directly on the soul and on how people behave, so the choice of music shaped character.
Music had a primary role in Greek tragedy: a chorus of up to 15 men sang and danced, and an aulos player provided the music.
A papyrus fragment preserves a few lines of music from Euripides' tragedy Orestes, first staged in 408 BCE.

title: The Zeng bells and China's eight sounds
description: The Marquis Yi of Zeng's bronze bells (about 2,400 years old, two notes per bell, music-theory inscriptions) and the ba yin classification by material.

facts.text: In 1978 the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng in Suizhou, Hubei, yielded the world's largest, best-preserved set of bronze bells, about 2,400 years old.
Each Zeng bell follows a 'one bell, two tones' system: it sounds two different notes depending on where it is struck.
The bells carry 3,755 characters of music-theory inscriptions, the earliest surviving archaeological documents showing mathematical relationships in music.
China's ancient ba yin, or eight sounds, dating from the Western Zhou, sorted instruments by material: stone, earth, bamboo, metal, skin, silk, wood and gourd.

title: Early music in India
description: The Samaveda set Vedic verses to fixed melodies for ritual singing; the Natyashastra, attributed to Bharata, treated music as part of theatre.

facts.text: The Samaveda, the 'Knowledge of the Chants', gathers verses mostly from the older Rigveda and arranges them to be sung to fixed melodies during rituals.
A specialist priest, the udgatri, sang the Samaveda chants, stretching, repeating and pausing on syllables to fit the melody.
The Natyashastra, attributed to the sage Bharata and dated to the 1st century BCE to 3rd century CE, is a treatise on Sanskrit theatre covering dance, music and poetics.

title: Gregorian chant
description: Monophonic, rhythmically free liturgical chant of the Roman Catholic Church, sung for the Mass and the canonical hours.

facts.text: Gregorian chant is monophonic, or unison, liturgical music of the Roman Catholic Church: everyone sings one melody, with no chords beneath it.
Gregorian chant is rhythmically free: it follows the words instead of a strict, regular beat.
Chant accompanied the Mass and the canonical hours, eight prayer services from Matins to Compline that early monastic communities set through the day.
In 1994 Chant, an album by the Benedictine monks of Santo Domingo de Silos in Spain, reached No. 3 on the Billboard 200.

title: Where Gregorian chant came from
description: Named after Pope Gregory I (590-604), the chant took its lasting shape when Charlemagne imposed it in Frankish lands and it merged with Gallican chant.

facts.text: Gregorian chant is named after Pope Gregory I (590-604), during whose papacy tradition says it was collected and codified.
Charlemagne, king of the Franks (768-814), imposed the chant on his kingdom, where it merged with the local Gallican chant in the 8th and 9th centuries.

title: Neumes
description: Early chant signs that reminded singers of melodies they had memorized; heighted neumes hinted at the melody's shape.

facts.text: Early staffless neumes, signs written above the words, only helped singers recall a melody they had already memorized by ear.
Scribes then heighted neumes, placing them higher or lower to suggest the melody's shape; on a staff, from about 1000, they showed exact pitch.

title: Guido's staff and syllables
description: Guido of Arezzo's four-line staff with letter clefs fixed pitch, and his ut-re-mi syllables from Ut queant laxis taught sight-singing.

facts.text: Guido of Arezzo (c. 990-1050), an Italian monk, used a four-line staff with letters as clefs, so singers no longer had to learn melodies by rote.
Guido claimed his system cut the 10 years normally needed to become a church singer to one year.
Guido took the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la from the hymn Ut queant laxis, whose lines begin on successively higher notes.
The syllable ut was later replaced by do, considered easier to sing, and si (later ti) was added for the seventh note.

title: Troubadours
description: Poet-musicians of southern France and nearby lands (late 11th to late 13th century) who wrote words and music in Occitan, favored at courts.

facts.text: Troubadours were lyric poet-musicians of southern France, northern Spain and northern Italy, from the late 11th to the late 13th century, writing in Occitan (langue d'oc).
William IX, duke of Aquitaine, born in 1071, is the earliest troubadour whose poems survive.
The word troubadour comes from the Occitan trobar, 'to find' or 'to invent'.
Troubadours were favored at noble courts, where their poems of love surrounded the ladies of the court with an aura of refinement.
Poet-musicians who also wrote their own words and music followed: trouvères in northern France and Minnesingers in Germany.

title: How troubadour songs survived
description: About 2,600 troubadour poems survive but fewer than 300 melodies; the Comtessa de Dia's A chantar is the only trobairitz song with its music.

facts.text: About 2,600 poems by some 450 troubadours survive, copied into songbooks called chansonniers, but fewer than 300 melodies do.
The Comtessa de Dia, probably named Beatriz (active around 1175), was a trobairitz, a woman troubadour; her A chantar is the only trobairitz song surviving with its music.

title: Polyphony and organum
description: Polyphony is two or more independent melodic lines at once; it began as organum, a second voice added to chant, first described in Musica enchiriadis (c. 900).

facts.text: Polyphony is two or more melodic lines sounding at once and heard as independent; monophony is a single line, as in chant.
The treatise Musica enchiriadis (c. 900) first describes organum: a voice added to a chant, the two moving note against note.
In early organum the added voice often doubled the chant a fourth or a fifth below.

title: Notre-Dame and the first great polyphony
description: Léonin's two-voice Magnus liber organi (c. 1170), Pérotin's three- and four-voice organa at Notre-Dame, and Machaut's four-voice Mass.

facts.text: At Notre-Dame in Paris, Léonin, the first major composer known by name, is credited with the Magnus liber organi (c. 1170), a book of two-voice organum.
His successor Pérotin wrote organa for three and four voices, including the four-voice Viderunt and Sederunt, when church music was almost all two-part.
Guillaume de Machaut (c. 1300-1377) wrote the Messe de Notre Dame for four voices, the first polyphonic setting of the Mass Ordinary by a single composer.

title: Josquin des Prez
description: Josquin (c. 1450-1521) worked between cathedrals, courts and the papal chapel; Luther called him the master of the notes.

facts.text: Martin Luther said Josquin was the master of the notes, which must do as he wishes, while other composers must do as the notes wish.
Josquin des Prez (c. 1450-1521) worked at Cambrai cathedral, the Sforza court in Milan, the papal chapel in Rome (1486-1494) and the court of Ferrara.
Josquin excelled at masses and motets for the church and at chansons, secular songs.

title: Madrigals and word painting
description: The madrigal, a secular song for several voices, used word painting to act out its text; England built a strong madrigal tradition.

facts.text: The madrigal was a secular vocal form, and late-16th-century madrigals featured vivid word painting, music that acts out the meaning of the words.
In Weelkes' 1601 madrigal As Vesta Was from Latmos Hill Descending, the notes descend on 'descending', rise on 'ascending', and 'all alone' gets a single voice.
It appeared in The Triumphes of Oriana (1603), England's most significant madrigal collection, dedicated to Queen Elizabeth I.

title: The Palestrina legend
description: A 1607 story that Palestrina's Pope Marcellus Mass saved church polyphony after the Council of Trent, a gross exaggeration.

facts.text: After the Council of Trent closed in 1563, Counter-Reformation reformers pressed for sacred words that listeners could clearly understand.
A 1607 treatise began the legend that Palestrina's Pope Marcellus Mass single-handedly saved church polyphony; musicologists call it a gross exaggeration.
Palestrina (c. 1525-1594) was known for keeping sung words clear to the ear, even amid intricate lines for several voices.

title: Petrucci prints polyphony
description: In Venice in 1501 Ottaviano Petrucci printed the Odhecaton, the first polyphonic music from movable type, using separate impressions for staff, notes and words.

facts.text: Johannes Gutenberg printed his Bible around 1455 on Europe's first known mechanized printing press.
Ottaviano Petrucci's Harmonice Musices Odhecaton A, printed in Venice in 1501, was the first polyphonic music printed from movable type.
Petrucci's method ran each sheet through the press several times: once for the staff lines, once for the notes and once for the words.
Petrucci produced 61 music publications, including works by Josquin des Prez.
Of Josquin's 20 surviving masses, 17 were printed in his lifetime by Petrucci, in 1502, 1505 and 1514.

title: Single-impression printing
description: Pierre Attaingnant's Paris type (1528) combined each note with a piece of staff, printing music in one pass, halving the work.

facts.text: In Paris, Pierre Attaingnant's Chansons nouvelles (1528) used type in which each piece combined a note with its own fragment of staff, printed in one impression.
Attaingnant's single-impression method halved the time and labor of printing music and was quickly adopted throughout Europe.

title: The Seikilos song
description: A Greek song carved with its melody on a marble tombstone from Tralles (1st or 2nd century CE), widely considered the oldest complete composition.

facts.text: The Seikilos epitaph, dated to the 1st or 2nd century CE, is widely considered the oldest complete musical composition; older notated pieces survive only in fragments.
It is carved on a marble tombstone from ancient Tralles, near Aydın in Turkey, found in 1883 and now in the National Museum of Denmark.
Greek letters and signs written above its words give the melody, and the words say: while you live, shine; have no grief at all; life is short.

title: The Baroque era
description: Western music from about 1600 to about 1750, named after a misshapen pearl by critics who meant it as an insult; grand and dramatic, with a strong melody-bass polarity and new forms such as opera, oratorio and the concerto.

facts.text: The Baroque period in Western music lasted from about 1600 to about 1750.
The word baroque comes from the Portuguese barroco, an irregularly shaped pearl, and its early senses were pejorative: irregular, extravagant.
The earliest known use of 'baroque' for music was a satirical 1734 review of Rameau's opera Hippolyte et Aricie, complaining of dissonance and constant changes of key and meter.
Britannica describes the Baroque style as grand, dramatic and energetic, with a polarity between the melody and the bass line and an interest in expressive harmony.
Opera, oratorio and cantata were the Baroque's most important new vocal forms, and the sonata, concerto and overture were created for instruments.

title: Basso continuo
description: The Baroque's foundation: a bass line played by a low instrument while a harpsichordist or organist improvised chords from figures written under it.

facts.text: Basso continuo was a partly improvised accompaniment on a bass line: a low instrument such as a cello or bassoon played the bass while a harpsichordist or organist supplied the chords.
In the 17th and 18th centuries often only the continuo's bass line was written out, with small numbers (figures) indicating the chords for the keyboard player to improvise.

title: Bach and the fugue
description: Bach's specialty, the fugue, passes one theme (the subject) from voice to voice; his Well-Tempered Clavier sets a prelude and fugue in every major and minor key.

facts.text: A fugue systematically imitates one main theme, the subject: a single voice states it, then each of the other voices enters with it in turn as the lines sound together.
Britannica calls Bach's fugues unsurpassed in variety and perfection, written for every medium available to him.
Bach's The Well-Tempered Clavier has two books, the first from 1722, each with 24 preludes and fugues, one in every major and minor key.

title: Bach's life and revival
description: Bach led Leipzig's church music from 1723 until 1750 and was admired mainly as an organist; Mendelssohn's 1829 St. Matthew Passion began the Bach revival.

facts.text: Johann Sebastian Bach (1685-1750) was director of church music in Leipzig from 1723 until his death in 1750.
In his lifetime Bach was admired mainly as an outstanding harpsichordist, organist and expert on organ building; today he is regarded as one of the greatest composers in history.
On March 11, 1829, in Berlin, 20-year-old Felix Mendelssohn conducted the first performance of Bach's St. Matthew Passion since Bach's death, launching the 19th-century Bach revival.

title: Vivaldi and the concerto
description: Vivaldi, the Red Priest who taught at Venice's Pietà, wrote about 500 concertos and fixed the concerto's fast-slow-fast shape, with orchestral refrains around solo passages.

facts.text: Antonio Vivaldi (1678-1741) of Venice was a priest nicknamed Il Prete Rosso, 'the Red Priest', for his reddish hair.
From 1703 Vivaldi was violin master at Venice's Ospedale della Pietà, a home for foundlings that specialized in musical training for its girls.
Vivaldi wrote about 500 concertos and established the concerto's three-movement, fast-slow-fast pattern.
Vivaldi was the first to use ritornello form regularly: a refrain for the full orchestra alternating with solo passages.
The Four Seasons is scored for solo violin, strings and basso continuo; the 1725 edition printed separate parts, including one for organ and cello together.

title: The Four Seasons as program music
description: The Four Seasons (published 1725) paints scenes from sonnets printed with the music, an early example of program music; it was little known until Kaufman's 1947 recording.

facts.text: The Four Seasons was virtually unknown before violinist Louis Kaufman's 1947 recording, which helped launch Vivaldi's modern fame.
The Four Seasons are four violin concertos, one per season, published in Amsterdam in 1725 as the first four of the 12 concertos of Vivaldi's Opus 8.
Each Four Seasons concerto came with a sonnet, possibly by Vivaldi himself, printed with the music, with letters marking where each scene happens.
Program music is music set to scenes or stories, and The Four Seasons is an example of it.
The Four Seasons sonnets and music depict birdsong and a thunderstorm in Spring, heat and a hailstorm in Summer, a harvest feast and a hunt in Autumn, and shivering and slipping on ice in Winter.

title: Handel and the English oratorio
description: Handel, born in 1685 like Bach, wrote Italian opera in London until the fashion faded, then turned to the English oratorio: a sacred drama for soloists, chorus and orchestra, sung without stage action.

facts.text: George Frideric Handel was born in Halle, Germany, in 1685, the same year as Bach, made his career in London and became a British subject in 1727.

Handel composed most of the Italian operas staged in London by the Royal Academy of Music from 1720 to 1728, but the form declined, partly as English audiences tired of entertainment in a language they could not understand.
An oratorio is a large-scale musical work on a sacred or semisacred subject for solo voices, chorus and orchestra.
Handel's English oratorios were sung by opera singers in theaters but without stage action.

title: Handel's Messiah
description: Messiah, set in 24 days in 1741 to a Bible text compiled by Charles Jennens, premiered in Dublin at Easter 1742; the King George II standing story is an unconfirmed legend.

facts.text: Handel composed Messiah in 24 days in 1741, setting a text compiled from the Bible by his friend Charles Jennens.
Messiah premiered in Dublin on April 13, 1742, at Easter rather than at Christmastime, when it is popularly played today, and the concert benefited three local charities.
The story that King George II stood during the Hallelujah chorus, starting the custom of standing, is a legend that can't be documented.

title: How opera began
description: Florence's Camerata tried to revive ancient Greek music and helped create monody; Peri's La Dafne (1598) was probably the first opera, and opera went public in Venice in 1637.

facts.text: In Florence about 1573-87, the Camerata, a circle of intellectuals, poets and musicians meeting under Count Giovanni Bardi, worked to revive ancient Greek music, and their work fed into the creation of opera.
Members of the Camerata included Vincenzo Galilei, the father of the astronomer Galileo.
The Camerata's efforts helped produce monody, expressive solo song with a simple chordal accompaniment, a dramatic style quite different from Renaissance polyphony.
Jacopo Peri's La Dafne (1598) was probably the first opera, and his L'Euridice (1600) is the first opera whose music survives complete.
Claudio Monteverdi's Orfeo, first performed at Mantua in 1607, was the first opera to keep a place in the modern repertory.
Europe's first public opera house, the San Cassiano Theatre, opened in Venice in 1637, taking opera beyond royal and noble patrons.

title: Recitative and aria
description: Opera sings its story in two modes: recitative follows the rhythm of speech and moves the plot; the aria pauses for emotion. Handel's Messiah uses the same tools.

facts.text: Recitative imitates the rhythms and accents of speech, using only a few pitches, and carries the dialogue and plot, while the aria is where emotion pours out in lyrical melody.
In Messiah, recitatives move the story forward and set up the arias and choruses.

title: How the orchestra grew
description: From Monteverdi's Orfeo and Lully's string-heavy court orchestra to Mannheim's four sections; the continuo dropped away after about 1770 and 19th-century orchestras added more winds and brass.

facts.text: Monteverdi's Orfeo (1607) used an orchestra of about 40 instruments, and for the first time a composer specified exactly which instruments to use at dramatic moments.
In the late 17th century Jean-Baptiste Lully directed an orchestra dominated by stringed instruments for the French royal court.
The 18th-century Mannheim court orchestra was famous across Europe for disciplined virtuosity and effects such as long crescendos; the music historian Charles Burney called it an 'army of generals'.
The Mannheim school established the basic makeup of the modern symphony orchestra: four sections, woodwinds, brass, percussion and strings.
As wind instruments gained independent parts after about 1770, the basso continuo became redundant and was abandoned.
In the 19th century orchestras grew: woodwinds went from two to typically three or four of each instrument, and the brass section gained more trumpets and horns plus trombones.

title: Why orchestras got a conductor
description: Baroque ensembles were led from the keyboard or first violin; as the continuo vanished and orchestras grew, a standing conductor with a baton took over (widely from about 1820), stressing the beat for everyone.

facts.text: In Bach's and Handel's time the composer usually led performances from the organ or harpsichord, and at the Paris Opera the concertmaster led from the first violin desk.
Lully died in 1687 of an infected wound in his foot caused by the long stick he used to beat time.
Batons came into wide use for orchestras only around 1820, when Louis Spohr brought the practice from Germany to London.
A conductor stresses the musical pulse so that all the performers follow the same meter, and uses the left hand to cue entries.

title: The Classical symphony
description: A symphony is a long orchestral work in several movements, typically four in the Classical era (fast, slow, minuet, fast); it grew from the Italian opera overture, and Haydn's 100-plus symphonies shaped it.

facts.text: A symphony is a lengthy work for orchestra in several movements; the typical Classical symphony has four: a fast opening movement, a slow movement, a minuet and a fast finale.
The symphony grew out of the Italian opera overture, the fast-slow-fast sinfonia played before an opera.
The minuet is an elegant couple dance in moderate triple time, such as 3/4, and is typically the third movement of a Classical symphony or string quartet.
Haydn wrote more than 100 symphonies and is known as the Father of the Symphony, though symphonies existed before him.
Haydn's Surprise Symphony, No. 94, premiered in London in 1792, is named for a startlingly loud chord that interrupts its soft, gentle slow movement.

title: Haydn at Esterhaza
description: Haydn served the Esterházy princes for nearly 30 years, isolated enough to be 'forced to become original'; his Farewell Symphony asked the prince, in music, to let the musicians go home.

facts.text: In Haydn's Farewell Symphony (1772), written when the musicians were homesick at the prince's summer palace, the players stop one by one in the finale, blow out their candles and leave; the prince took the hint and let them go.
Joseph Haydn (1732-1809) worked for the Esterházy princes for nearly 30 years from 1761.
Haydn said that, cut off from the world at Eszterháza with nobody to confuse him, he was 'forced to become original'.

title: Mozart's life and works
description: Mozart (1756-1791) was composing at five and touring Europe from 1763; he wrote more than 600 works, including Figaro, Don Giovanni and The Magic Flute, and died at 35 with his Requiem unfinished.

facts.text: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in Salzburg on January 27, 1756, and died in Vienna on December 5, 1791, at 35.
At three Mozart was picking out chords on the harpsichord, at four playing short pieces, and at five composing.
Mozart's father Leopold, a violinist and composer, took Wolfgang and his gifted sister Nannerl on tours of Europe from 1763, including Paris and London.
Mozart composed more than 600 works, including the operas The Marriage of Figaro (1786), Don Giovanni (1787) and The Magic Flute (1791).
Mozart left his Requiem unfinished when he died, and his student Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it.

title: Mozart myths
description: Two popular Mozart stories are myths: Salieri did not poison him (the legend grew through Pushkin and Amadeus), and research finds no Mozart-specific 'Mozart effect' on intelligence.

facts.text: There is no foundation for the belief that Salieri poisoned Mozart; the legend fed Pushkin's drama Mozart and Salieri and later Peter Shaffer's play Amadeus, filmed in 1984.
Salieri was an important teacher whose students included Beethoven, Franz Schubert and Franz Liszt.

A 1993 study found college students did better on a spatial task after hearing Mozart; a 2010 University of Vienna analysis of about 40 studies with over 3,000 people found no support for a Mozart-specific gain.

title: The string quartet
description: Two violins, a viola and a cello, one player per part and no conductor; developed largely by Haydn from about 1750 into an intimate conversation among equals.

facts.text: A string quartet is made up of two violins, a viola and a cello.
Chamber music is written for small ensembles, most often with no more than one player to a part, and it usually does without a conductor.
The string quartet owes its development largely to Haydn, known as the Father of the String Quartet, and from about 1750 it became chamber music's principal medium.
The Classical string quartet was an intimate, closely built dialogue among equals and challenging to play; Goethe later described it as 'four rational people conversing'.
Haydn's Opus 33 quartets and Mozart's six quartets dedicated to Haydn became the prototype that later quartets were long measured against.

title: Haydn, Mozart and the quartet
description: Haydn and Mozart played quartets together; in 1785 Mozart dedicated six quartets to Haydn, who told Leopold Mozart that Wolfgang was the greatest composer he knew.

facts.text: In the 1780s Haydn and Mozart played string quartets together, Haydn on violin and Mozart on viola.
In 1785 Mozart dedicated six string quartets to Haydn, an unusual gesture since dedications usually went to wealthy patrons.
After hearing the quartets in 1785, Haydn told Mozart's father Leopold that his son was the greatest composer he knew, in person or by reputation.

title: Baroque versus Classical
description: Late-Baroque music favored intricate polyphony over a continuo; the Classical style (the later 18th century) reacted with melody-led homophony, simplicity and clarity.

facts.text: Reacting against the intricate polyphony of the late Baroque, Classical composers made a homophonic texture dominated by melody the norm.
Classical-style form was marked by simplicity and clarity, and its melodies became more tuneful.
Haydn and Mozart, with Beethoven, brought the Viennese Classical school of the later 18th century to its height.

title: Beethoven, the bridge
description: Beethoven kept Classical forms but stretched them to carry a personal vision (the Eroica, the Fifth's minor-to-major journey, the choral Ninth), bridging the Classical and Romantic eras.

facts.text: Beethoven, baptized in Bonn in December 1770, left for Vienna in autumn 1792, aged 21, to study with Haydn, and never returned to Bonn.
Beethoven died in Vienna on 26 March 1827.
Britannica calls Beethoven the predominant musical figure in the transitional period between the Classical and Romantic eras.
Beethoven planned to dedicate his Third Symphony to Napoleon; after Napoleon had himself named emperor in December 1804, Beethoven tore the title page away, and the work became Eroica, heroic.
The Eroica, premiered in Vienna in 1805, was grander and more dramatic than symphonies of its time and introduced the idea that a symphony could present its creator's view of the world.
At the Eroica's 1805 premiere, one listener reportedly complained he would pay extra if it would only stop.
Beethoven's Fifth Symphony (premiered 1808) opens with three short Gs and a long E-flat, short-short-short-long, and travels from C minor to a finale in C major.
Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, premiered in Vienna in 1824, ends with a full chorus and solo singers setting Schiller's poem Ode to Joy, the first time a major composer put voices in a symphony.

title: Beethoven's hearing loss
description: Beethoven's deafness came on gradually: weakening hearing and ringing from about 1798, lost high notes by 1801, the private Heiligenstadt Testament of 1802, conversation books from 1818, profound deafness by the Ninth's 1824 premiere. He kept composing by inner hearing.

facts.text: In an 1801 letter to his friend Franz Wegeler, Beethoven wrote that his hearing had been growing weaker for three years (so since about 1798) and that from a distance he couldn't hear the high notes of instruments and singers.
Beethoven's early symptoms included buzzing and ringing in his ears (tinnitus) along with the loss of high pitches.
In October 1802, aged 31, Beethoven wrote a letter to his brothers Carl and Johann at Heiligenstadt near Vienna; he kept it private, and it was found among his papers after his death in 1827.
In the Heiligenstadt Testament, Beethoven explained that his withdrawal came from hiding his deafness, and wrote that he had come close to ending his life and only his art held him back.
By about 1814 Beethoven was nearly deaf in his right ear and tried ear trumpets made for him by Johann Nepomuk Maelzel.
From 1818 Beethoven used conversation books: visitors wrote their side of the conversation and he usually answered aloud; more than 130 survive.
Though profoundly deaf, Beethoven went on composing masterworks such as the Ninth Symphony and his late string quartets, relying on his inner hearing.
At the Ninth's 1824 premiere, Beethoven stood on stage giving tempos while Michael Umlauf led the orchestra; unable to hear the applause, he was turned around by a singer to see it.

title: Romantic music puts emotion first
description: Romanticism (late 18th to mid-19th century) exalted emotion over reason and the individual; in music it brought emotionalism, individualism, nationalism, richer harmony and new forms for personal expression.

facts.text: Romanticism, from the late 18th to the mid-19th century, emphasized the individual, the imaginative and the emotional, exalting emotion over reason and the senses over intellect.
Britannica says Romantic music embraced emotionalism, individualism and nationalism, with richer harmony and new forms for intense personal expression.

title: Program music
description: Program music is instrumental music that carries a story, scene or idea beyond the notes; Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique (1830) came with a printed program and turned the beloved into a recurring melody, the idée fixe.

facts.text: Program music is instrumental music that carries an extramusical meaning, such as a story, legend, scene or personal drama; absolute music, its opposite, is sound for its own sake.
At the 5 December 1830 premiere of his Symphonie fantastique in Paris, Berlioz had a printed program of its story handed to the audience.
The Symphonie fantastique follows a lovesick artist through five movements, including a ball, a march to the scaffold and a witches' sabbath.

Berlioz loved the Irish actress Harriet Smithson from afar after seeing her as Ophelia; in the symphony the beloved becomes a recurring melody, the idée fixe, grotesquely transformed in the witches' sabbath.
Berlioz married Harriet Smithson in 1833.

title: Chopin and the piano
description: Chopin, born near Warsaw in 1810 and settled in Paris from 1831, wrote almost only for piano, including mazurkas and polonaises tied to his Polish feeling; he preferred intimate settings, and his heart was returned to Warsaw.

facts.text: Chopin was born near Warsaw in 1810, left Poland in 1830 and settled in Paris in 1831; he never returned to Poland.
Chopin died in Paris in 1849, aged 39; he was buried at Père-Lachaise, but his heart was taken to Warsaw's Church of the Holy Cross.
Chopin wrote little but piano music, including nocturnes, polonaises and dozens of mazurkas; Britannica ties the mazurkas and polonaises to his strong nationalist feeling.
Chopin's delicate touch did not suit large concert halls, and he preferred playing in intimate settings.
In Paris, Chopin and Franz Liszt were friends.
The mazurka is a Polish folk dance for couples, with stamping feet and clicking heels, in triple time with a strong accent on the second beat.

title: Rubato
description: Rubato, 'robbed time', stretches some beats and hurries others for expression; in Chopin's style the left hand keeps a fairly steady tempo while the right hand bends the melody.

facts.text: Rubato, from the Italian rubare, 'to rob', means stretching some beats or phrases and hurrying others for expression.
In Chopin's rubato, the left hand keeps a fairly steady tempo while the right hand bends, stretches or nudges the melody.

title: Paganini, Liszt and the virtuoso
description: Paganini's violin playing seemed so impossible that rumors of a pact with the devil spread; Liszt set out to do the same on piano, gave the first complete solo recitals (the word first used for his 1840 London concerts) and inspired 'Lisztomania'.

facts.text: Paganini's playing seemed so extraordinary that stories circulated that he was in league with the devil and had been imprisoned for murder.
Paganini, born in Genoa in 1782, wrote 24 Caprices for solo violin that showcase techniques such as harmonics and pizzicato.
Paganini's concert tours made him famous across Europe, and his appearances in Paris and London in 1831 were sensational.
After hearing Paganini play, the Hungarian-born pianist Franz Liszt resolved to transfer Paganini's violin effects to the piano.
Liszt gave the first complete solo piano recitals; his 1840 London concerts, billed as 'Liszt's Pianoforte Recitals', were the first time 'recital' was used for music rather than dramatic readings.
In 1844 the poet Heinrich Heine coined the word 'Lisztomania'; drawings of the time show women swooning and flowers thrown at the stage.

title: Verdi and Italian opera
description: Verdi paired great drama with memorable melody; Nabucco (1842) made him Italy's operatic hero at 28, its chorus 'Va, pensiero' became an unofficial anthem, and he was still writing at 79 with Falstaff.

facts.text: After his comic opera Un giorno di regno failed, Verdi's Nabucco (1842) succeeded sensationally and made him, at 28, the new hero of Italian music.
In Nabucco, Hebrew exiles sing 'Va, pensiero', longing for their lost homeland; the chorus later became an unofficial Italian national anthem.
Historians debate how much Verdi's operas stirred Italian patriots at first; the link between his music and nationalism may have formed more gradually than often claimed.
When Verdi's remains were moved in Milan in 1901, a choir of 820 voices led by Arturo Toscanini sang 'Va, pensiero'.
Verdi drew his operas from great drama by Shakespeare, Victor Hugo, Byron and Schiller, pairing powerful theater with memorable melody.
Verdi's operas include Rigoletto (1851), La traviata (1853) and Aida (1871), which premiered in Cairo.
Verdi's Falstaff, after Shakespeare, premiered at La Scala in 1893 when he was 79; his only other comedy had failed there half a century earlier.

title: Wagner's music drama
description: Wagner fused poetry and music into continuous music drama, built his own Bayreuth theater with a hidden orchestra, and staged the 15-hour Ring there in 1876. He also published antisemitic writing, a documented and disputed part of his legacy.

facts.text: Richard Wagner was born in Leipzig in 1813, the same year as Verdi.
Wagner conceived music drama as poetic drama set to one continuous vocal-symphonic texture, rather than a string of separate set pieces.
Wagner's Ring of the Nibelung is four operas totaling about 15 hours of music, first performed complete at Bayreuth in August 1876.
Wagner's festival theater at Bayreuth, built to his design, opened in 1876; its orchestra plays in a pit hidden beneath the stage so that nothing distracts from the drama.
A leitmotif ('leading motive') is a short musical idea tied to a character, object or idea, which Wagner's orchestra develops as the drama unfolds.
Wagner published antisemitic writing, notably the essay 'Judaism in Music' (1850, first under a pseudonym, reissued under his name in 1869), blaming Jewish musicians for what he saw as empty music.

Britannica notes Wagner's antisemitism has been used to explain why he was a favorite composer of Adolf Hitler and to justify an unofficial ban on his music in Israel; its role in his music remains disputed.

title: Music and nations
description: Nationalism in Romantic music meant revealing and glorifying a nation's distinctive features, drawing on folk tunes, dances, folklore and village life: Smetana's Vltava paints a Czech river; Sibelius's Finlandia had to hide from Russian censors.

facts.text: Nationalism in Romantic music meant revealing and glorifying a nation's distinctive features, drawing on folk tunes, folk dances, folklore and village life.
Leaders of musical nationalism included Glinka in Russia, Smetana and Dvořák for Czech music, and Grieg in Norway.

Smetana's Vltava (The Moldau), completed in 1874, follows the river from its source in the Bohemian Forest past hunters and a village wedding in polka rhythm to Prague; it is the second of the six parts of Má vlast (My Country).
Smetana became totally deaf in late 1874, and he wrote Má vlast between then and 1879.

Sibelius's Finlandia was written in 1899 for a veiled rally for press freedom in Finland, then under tsarist Russia; to avoid censors, early performances sometimes used titles like 'Impromptu' or 'Happy Feelings at the Awakening of Finnish Spring'.

title: Tchaikovsky's ballets
description: Tchaikovsky wrote ballet music with symphonic drama: Swan Lake flopped in Moscow in 1877 and succeeded only in the 1895 Petipa-Ivanov revival after his death; The Nutcracker (1892) introduced the celesta as the Sugar Plum Fairy's voice.

facts.text: Swan Lake's 1877 Bolshoi premiere in Moscow was poorly received: critics rejected the music as too dramatic and emotional, like Wagner's dark style, when audiences expected light, airy ballet scores.
Tchaikovsky died in St. Petersburg in 1893.
In 1895 Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov restaged Swan Lake at the Mariinsky Theatre in St. Petersburg; their version is the one most often followed today.

Tchaikovsky found the celesta in Paris, calling it something between a piano and a glockenspiel, asked his publisher to keep it secret from Rimsky-Korsakov and Glazunov, and made it the Sugar Plum Fairy's voice in The Nutcracker (St. Petersburg, 1892).

title: The Romantics revive Bach
description: On 11 March 1829 in Berlin, the 20-year-old Mendelssohn conducted Bach's St. Matthew Passion, its first performance since Bach's death, launching the 19th-century Bach revival.

facts.text: On 11 March 1829 at the Singakademie in Berlin, Felix Mendelssohn, aged 20, conducted Bach's St. Matthew Passion, its first performance since Bach's death in 1750.
Britannica says Mendelssohn's 1829 performance inaugurated the Bach revival of the 19th century.

title: How musical traditions differ
description: Musical traditions differ in their scales, their ways of organizing time and their instruments, as the 1977 Voyager Golden Record's mix of gamelan, drumming, raga and shakuhachi shows.

facts.text: Launched in 1977, both Voyager spacecraft carry a golden record into interstellar space, with an eclectic 90-minute selection of music chosen for NASA by a committee chaired by Carl Sagan.
The Voyager record's music includes a Javanese court gamelan piece, percussion from Senegal, an Indian raga sung by Kesarbai Kerkar and a Japanese shakuhachi solo, alongside Bach and Chuck Berry.
In Indian classical music, time is organized by tala, a metric cycle of a fixed number of beats that recurs throughout a performance and has no exact equivalent in Western music.
Polyrhythm, combining contrasting rhythms, is a key feature of much African music, often over timeline patterns played on instruments such as bells.
The gamelan, the orchestra of Java and Bali in Indonesia, consists largely of gongs and tuned metal instruments struck with mallets.

title: Ethnomusicology
description: Ethnomusicology studies all the world's musics, each in its own context and largely through fieldwork; Smithsonian Folkways has documented the world's 'people's music' since 1948.

facts.text: Ethnomusicology is the study of all the world's musics; the term was introduced around 1950 by the Dutch scholar Jaap Kunst and American scholars, replacing 'comparative musicology'.
Ethnomusicology depends on field research, including the direct study of music performance.
Moses Asch founded Folkways Records in 1948 to document 'people's music' and sounds from around the world; the Smithsonian acquired it in 1987.

title: Raga
description: A raga is a melodic framework: a set of notes with a typical order and characteristic motifs, within which Indian classical musicians improvise, over a tambura drone.

facts.text: South Asian classical music has two principal types: Hindustani, found mainly in the north, and Carnatic, in the south.
A raga is based on a set of notes, sometimes differing going up and coming down, with a typical order in which they appear and characteristic motifs.
Several hundred ragas are in present use, and thousands are possible in theory.
Northern Indian musicians classify ragas by mood, season and time of day, associations that modern concert practice largely disregards.
Raga performances mix improvisation and memorized compositions, using only the raga's tones.
A typical Hindustani performance, which may last well over an hour, begins with a long nonmetric improvisation called alap.
The tambura, a long-necked lute, is used only to play the supporting drone, a single repeated chord.
The sitar is a long-necked fretted lute with about 30 melodic, drone and sympathetic strings.

title: Tala
description: Tala is the rhythmic cycle of Indian classical music: tintal has 16 beats in four groups, kept with claps and waves, played on tabla, and resolving on the sam, the first beat.

facts.text: Tintal, one of the most performed Hindustani talas, has 16 beats in four groups of four; performers keep the tala with claps and waves of the hand.
The sam, the first beat of a tala cycle, is its point of maximum rhythmic resolution.
Drummers and soloists play rhythmic patterns that contradict the tala but eventually return to its basic scheme.
The tabla is a set of two drums played by one musician, the right-hand drum carefully tuned.

title: Gamelan tuning: slendro and pelog
description: Each gamelan is tuned only to itself. A full Javanese set is a double set in two tunings: slendro (five near-equal steps) and pelog (seven unequal pitches, used in sets of five).

facts.text: Each gamelan is tuned to its own ensemble rather than to an external pitch standard, so instruments are not interchangeable between sets.
A full Javanese gamelan is a double set, one in slendro tuning and one in pelog, and the two sets are never played simultaneously.
Slendro has five notes per octave, with intervals so close in size that they are often described as equal or nearly equal.
Pelog has seven pitches per octave with clearly narrow and wide intervals, but pieces are built on sets of five of those pitches.

title: The gamelan ensemble and its gong cycles
description: Javanese gamelan combines gongs, metallophones, drums, strings, flute and voices, and it moves in cycles: the great gong ageng marks the end of each gongan.

facts.text: A full Javanese gamelan also includes kendhang drums that guide the music's flow, the bowed rebab, the gambang xylophone, the suling bamboo flute and singers.
Gamelan is played for its own sake and also accompanies dance drama and the wayang shadow puppet play, at rites of passage and communal festivals.
In Javanese gamelan, a stroke of the large hanging gong, the gong ageng, marks the end of the main musical unit, the gongan; the kenong, kempul and kethuk gongs subdivide it.

title: Talking drums
description: West African talking drums such as the Yoruba dundun imitate speech: squeezing the drum's cords changes its pitch, following the tones of a tonal language.

facts.text: Among the Yoruba of Nigeria, dundun drums are used as talking drums to accompany oriki, praise-name poetry.
Talking drums imitate the rhythm and the rise and fall of words in a language; examples include the Yoruba dundun and the Asante atumpan.
The talking drum is an hourglass-shaped pressure drum with cords running between its two heads; the player holds it under the arm and squeezes the cords, tightening the head and changing its pitch.
Yoruba is a tonal language, in which the pitch of a syllable can change a word's meaning; skilled talking drummers imitate tonal languages and reproduce proverbs and praise songs.

title: The bell time line in Ewe drumming
description: In Agbadza, the music of the Ewe of Ghana and Togo, a repeating bell phrase (2+2+1+2+2+2+1) is the time line that keeps every drum part in polyrhythmic alignment.

facts.text: Agbadza, music and dance of the Ewe people of Ghana and Togo, is widely regarded by other ethnic groups as the main type of Ewe music and dance.
Agbadza's drum ensemble sets the low lead sogo drum and the response kidi drum against the gankogui bell, the axatse rattle, the kagan drum and handclaps.
Agbadza's recurring bell phrase, 2+2+1+2+2+2+1, is a time line widespread in West Africa; it gives every player a reference for correct polyrhythmic alignment.

title: Griots
description: Griots (jeli or jali) are hereditary West African musician-historians who keep genealogies and oral history alive, many playing the 21-string kora.

facts.text: Griots, called jeli or jali in Mande languages, are hereditary West African troubadour-historians who preserve genealogies, historical narratives and oral traditions and sing praise songs; they have also served as advisers and diplomats.
Many griots play the kora, a long-necked harp-lute with 21 strings and a calabash gourd resonator, played with four fingers.

title: The oud
description: The oud, a short-necked fretless lute with a pear-shaped body, is central to Middle Eastern music and is the parent of the European lute, whose name comes from Arabic al-'ud.

facts.text: The English word 'lute' comes, through French and Old Occitan, from Arabic al-'ud, literally 'the wood', the name of the oud.
The oud, prominent in medieval and modern Islamic music, is the parent of the European lute.
The oud has a deep pear-shaped body, a fretless fingerboard and a relatively short neck, and its strings are plucked with a plectrum.
Four pairs of strings are the classical number on an oud, although five and six pairs are also found.
The oud's present form probably emerged in Andalusia in Muslim Spain, with a separate neck and round sound hole.

title: Maqam
description: Maqam is the melodic system of the Middle East and parts of North Africa: pitches, characteristic motifs and rules of use, including three-quarter tones, explored in the taqsim.

facts.text: In the music of the Middle East and parts of North Africa, a maqam is a set of pitches and characteristic melodic motifs, with a traditional pattern for using them.
Maqam notes are separated by the half tones and whole tones of Western music and also by three-quarter and five-quarter tones.
About 50 maqamat survive, but a few are by far the most used, including rast, saba, nahawand, hijaz, 'ajam and sika.
In a taqsim, a prominent genre of Arabic music, the performer improvises, moving from the home maqam to others and eventually returning to the starting point.
Britannica describes maqam as similar to the Persian dastgah and roughly related to the Indian raga.

title: The erhu
description: The erhu is China's most popular bowed fiddle: two strings over a snakeskin-covered resonator, no fingerboard, and a bow whose hair runs between the strings.

facts.text: The erhu is a bowed, two-stringed Chinese vertical fiddle, the most popular of its class; held upright on the player's thigh, it has strings usually tuned a fifth apart over a snakeskin-covered wooden resonator, and no fingerboard.
On the erhu and related huqin fiddles, the bow hair passes between the strings.

title: The koto
description: The koto is a long Japanese zither with 13 strings over movable bridges, plucked with tsume picks, long called Japan's national instrument.

facts.text: The koto is a long Japanese board zither with 13 strings and movable bridges, related to the Chinese zheng and long known as Japan's national instrument.
Koto players pluck the strings with the thumb and first two fingers of the right hand, fitted with picks called tsume.

title: The shakuhachi
description: The shakuhachi is a Japanese end-blown bamboo flute named for its length; Edo-period Fuke Zen monks, the komuso, played it as meditation called suizen.

facts.text: The Voyager Golden Record includes the Japanese shakuhachi piece 'Tsuru No Sugomori' ('Crane's Nest'), performed by Goro Yamaguchi.

The shakuhachi is a Japanese end-blown bamboo flute with four finger holes and a thumbhole, derived from the Chinese xiao in the 8th century; its name comes from its length, one shaku and eight (hachi) sun.

In the Edo period, komuso ('monks of emptiness') of the Fuke sect of Zen Buddhism played the shakuhachi in public wearing straw-woven basket hats; its spiritual practice is called suizen, 'blowing Zen'.

title: Flamenco: song, dance and guitar
description: Flamenco, from Andalusia with an essential Gitano (Roma) role, fuses cante (song, its essence), baile (dance) and toque (guitar), with handclaps and footwork.

facts.text: Flamenco was inscribed in 2010 on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Andalusia in southern Spain is flamenco's heartland, and the Gitano (Roma) community has played an essential role in its development.
Flamenco fuses song (cante), dance (baile) and musicianship, especially guitar playing (toque).
The essence of flamenco is cante, song; its most profound category is cante jondo, 'deep song'.
Cante is sung by men and women, preferably seated and with no backing singers, and its brief, simple lyrics express feelings from grief and joy to tragedy and fear.
Flamenco's song-centered 'golden age' spanned roughly 1780 to 1845.
Flamenco guitar playing (toque) has long surpassed its original role as accompaniment; castanets, hand-clapping and foot-stamping are also used.
Dance has dominated flamenco since the mid-19th century, after cafes cantantes, commercial venues opening from 1842, shifted the focus to musicians and dancers.
Flamenco dance uses movements of the arms, upper torso, hands and fingers, along with footwork and heelwork.

title: Flamenco's compas
description: The compas is flamenco's 12-beat rhythmic cycle, with groups of three and two inside it, coordinating singers, guitarists and dancers in forms like soleares.

facts.text: The flamenco compas is a 12-beat measure into which groups of three and two are arranged and accented in traditional ways, coordinating singers, instrumentalists and dancers.
Soleares, a fundamental flamenco form considered cante jondo, is performed in a slow twelve-beat pattern.

title: Samba
description: Samba de roda grew from the traditions of enslaved Africans in Bahia, Brazil, and, carried to Rio de Janeiro, shaped the urban samba that became a national symbol.

facts.text: Samba de roda developed in the Reconcavo region of Bahia, Brazil, in the 17th century, drawing heavily on the dances and traditions of the region's enslaved Africans, with Portuguese language, poetry and some instruments.
In samba de roda, participants gather in a circle, the roda, clapping and singing while dancers take turns in the center.
Migrants took samba de roda to Rio de Janeiro, where it influenced the urban samba that became a symbol of Brazilian national identity in the 20th century.

title: Tango
description: Tango grew around 1880 among the urban lower classes of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, mixing European, African-descended and criollo traditions, and took Europe by storm by 1915.

facts.text: Tango was developed by the urban lower classes of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, on the Rio de la Plata, from a mix of European immigrants, descendants of enslaved Africans and criollos.
Tango evolved about 1880 in Buenos Aires, where the Spanish tango, a light-spirited variety of flamenco, merged with the Argentine milonga, with possible influence from the Cuban habanera.
By 1915 tango was a craze in fashionable European circles, and by 1920 its music and lyrics had become intensely melancholy.

title: Salsa and clave
description: Salsa ('sauce') is a hybrid built on Afro-Cuban music, especially the Cuban son, shaped in New York by Puerto Rican and Cuban musicians, and it runs on the clave pattern.

facts.text: Salsa, Spanish for 'sauce', is a hybrid form based on Afro-Cuban music, above all the Cuban son, which blended Spanish guitar traditions with African rhythmic elements.

Salsa developed in New York City, with major contributions from Puerto Rican musicians such as Tito Puente and Eddie Palmieri; Celia Cruz became the reigning diva of Afro-Cuban dance music in the 1960s, and salsa peaked in the 1970s.
The claves are two thick wooden sticks, and clave is also the rhythmic pattern played on them, the foundation of various forms of Afro-Cuban music.

title: Folk songs and oral tradition
description: Folk music lives in oral tradition: learned by ear within families and communities, it changes as it passes on, as Cecil Sharp found in Appalachia.

facts.text: Folk music is traditional, generally rural music originally passed down through families and other small social groups; it lives in oral tradition, learned through hearing rather than reading.
As folk songs are passed on they vary, changed by singers' creativity and forgetfulness, so that each performance can differ.

Between 1916 and 1918, the English folk-song collector Cecil Sharp and his assistant Maud Karpeles spent 46 weeks in the Southern Appalachians, collecting songs of English origin and others that were distinctly American.

title: Barbara Allen: one ballad, many versions
description: The ballad 'Barbara Allen', mentioned by Samuel Pepys in 1666, is one of the most collected folk songs, in so many versions that the Library of Congress issued a whole LP of them.

facts.text: In a diary entry of January 1666, Samuel Pepys wrote of the pleasure of hearing the actress Mrs. Knipp sing 'her little Scotch song of Barbary Allen'.
'Barbara Allen' (Child 84) is one of the ballads most often collected by folklore fieldworkers, under a variety of names and in many versions.
In 1966 the Library of Congress released the LP Versions and Variants of the Tunes of Barbara Allen, edited by Charles Seeger from its Archive of Folk Song.

title: From West African bell to Afro-Cuban clave
description: West African bell patterns crossed the Atlantic with enslaved Africans: a pattern heard in Ghana would be called son clave in Afro-Cuban music.

facts.text: A Smithsonian Folkways lesson teaches that West African polyrhythmic traditions followed Africans to the Caribbean as a result of the transatlantic slave trade.
Smithsonian Folkways notes that the pattern in 'Gome', from the album Folk Music of Ghana, would be called son clave if played in Afro-Cuban music.

title: Spirituals of enslaved African Americans
description: Spirituals are religious folk songs created by enslaved people of African descent in the American South, passed on only by live singing and often voicing a longing for freedom.

facts.text: Spirituals are religious folk songs created and sung by enslaved people of African descent in the American South.
Throughout the era of slavery, spirituals were passed from one generation to the next only by live, oral transmission.
'Go Down, Moses' retells the Exodus story with the call-and-response refrain 'Let my people go' and expresses enslaved people's longing for freedom.

title: Call-and-response in African American song
description: Spirituals and work songs are built for call-and-response: a leader sings a line and a group answers with a refrain.

facts.text: Spirituals are structured for call-and-response between a leader's line and a chorus's refrain, often over clapping and patting.
Many African American work crews had a song leader who sang a line, and the other workers answered with a refrain.

title: Work songs and their legacy
description: Work songs kept laborers in rhythm and passed the time; out of them, during and after slavery, came spirituals and eventually the blues.

facts.text: Work songs passed the time and coordinated workers' movements, keeping a regular rhythm for a task.
During and after slavery, Black American workers developed spirituals and, ultimately, the blues out of older work song traditions.

title: The Fisk Jubilee Singers
description: In 1871 a student choir from debt-ridden Fisk University toured to raise money, bringing spirituals to audiences in the US and Europe.

facts.text: Fisk University, founded in 1865 to educate formerly enslaved people, was deep in debt by 1871, when a professor formed a student choir to raise money.
