On an 1873 tour of Europe the Fisk Jubilee Singers sang for Queen Victoria, and tour proceeds built Fisk's Jubilee Hall.
The Jubilee Singers brought spirituals, rarely heard outside Black churches and homes, to audiences in the US and Europe.

title: Where the blues came from
description: African Americans created the blues in the Deep South after the Civil War, out of work songs, field calls and spirituals; W.C. Handy helped bring it to a national audience.

facts.text: African Americans created the blues in the Deep South after the Civil War; it was a recognizable genre by the 1890s.
The blues developed among formerly enslaved people and their descendants, many still working on Southern plantations.
The three-line blues form grew out of African American work songs, field calls, spirituals and folk ballads.
Around 1903, at the train station in Tutwiler, Mississippi, W.C. Handy heard a man singing while pressing a knife on his guitar strings.
W.C. Handy, known as the 'Father of the Blues', published 'The Memphis Blues' in 1912 and 'St. Louis Blues' in 1914.

title: The 12-bar blues and its AAB verse
description: Most blues use a 12-bar form on three chords, with three-line stanzas: a line, its repeat, and a rhyming answer.

facts.text: A blues stanza has three lines: the second more or less repeats the first, and the third finishes the thought with a new line that rhymes.
Most blues, and much jazz, use a 12-bar form built on three chords: the tonic, the subdominant and the dominant.

title: Blue notes
description: Blue notes lower the third, seventh and sometimes fifth by less than a semitone, landing between the major and minor pitches; guitarists bend or slide strings to reach them.

facts.text: A blue note is a microtonal lowering of the third, seventh and sometimes fifth of the major scale, so a blue third falls between major and minor.
Blues guitarists bend strings or slide a bottleneck or metal bar along them, following the voice and stressing the blue notes.

title: Ragtime's syncopation
description: Ragtime piano sets a syncopated right-hand melody against a steady left-hand beat; it led American popular music from about 1899 to 1917.

facts.text: Ragtime, a syncopated style and one forerunner of jazz, was the leading style of American popular music from about 1899 to 1917.
In ragtime piano the left hand keeps a steady, regularly accented beat while the right hand plays a syncopated melody.
Syncopation means accenting off the beat; to 'rag' a piece was to syncopate its melody.
Ragtime drew on African American banjo styles and the syncopated dance rhythms of the cakewalk.

title: Scott Joplin, King of Ragtime
description: Scott Joplin, an African American composer from Texas, became the King of Ragtime with 'Maple Leaf Rag' (1899), wrote an opera, and won a posthumous Pulitzer in 1976.

facts.text: Scott Joplin, an African American composer born in Texas in 1867 or 1868, became known as the 'King of Ragtime'.
Joplin's 'Maple Leaf Rag', published in 1899, was the most successful early rag and became ragtime's signature piece.
Joplin wrote a three-act opera, Treemonisha, and published it at his own expense in 1911.
After the film The Sting's Oscar-winning score revived his music in the 1970s, Joplin (died 1917) got a posthumous special Pulitzer in 1976.

title: Jazz begins in New Orleans
description: Jazz was developed by African Americans in New Orleans from brass bands, blues, spirituals and West African, Caribbean and Spanish traditions; 1890s segregation laws pushed Black and Creole musicians together.

facts.text: By the mid-1700s, enslaved people in New Orleans gathered on Sundays at a market later called Congo Square, famous for African dance and music.
Jazz grew from New Orleans brass bands, West African, Caribbean and Spanish traditions, and the blues and spirituals.
Jazz was developed by African Americans; its rhythms come mainly from West African traditions, its instruments, like trumpet and trombone, from Europe.
Segregation laws passed in the 1890s ended the special status of New Orleans Creoles of color and ultimately united Black and Creole musicians.
Between 1895 and 1900, New Orleans cornetist Buddy Bolden added improvised blues to dance tunes; his band is generally considered the first jazz band.
No recording of Buddy Bolden was ever made; his horn was said to carry for miles.

title: New Orleans collective improvisation
description: Early New Orleans bands had a front line of cornet, clarinet and trombone improvising together; the first commercial jazz record (1917) was made by a white band.

facts.text: Early New Orleans jazz bands had a front line of cornet, clarinet and trombone, improvising together over guitar, bass and drums.
In 1917 the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, five white musicians, made what is considered the first commercial jazz recording.

title: Louis Armstrong makes the solo central
description: On his Hot Five and Hot Seven records (1925-28), Armstrong broke from collective improvising and became the first great jazz soloist.

facts.text: Louis Armstrong, born in New Orleans in 1901, learned cornet in the band of the Colored Waifs Home, where he was sent in 1913.
In 1922 King Oliver, leading a band in Chicago, sent for Armstrong to play second cornet.
On his Hot Five and Hot Seven records of 1925-28, Armstrong left collective improvising behind and emerged as the first great jazz soloist.
By 'West End Blues' (1928), Armstrong had made the virtuoso soloist preeminent in jazz; he influenced virtually all later jazz horn players.
Armstrong made the recordings that revolutionized jazz in Chicago between 1925 and 1928.

title: Scat singing
description: Armstrong helped invent scat singing, using wordless syllables instead of lyrics; 'Heebie Jeebies' is one of the earliest scat recordings.

facts.text: Armstrong helped invent scat singing, wordless syllables in place of lyrics, and made one of the earliest scat recordings, 'Heebie Jeebies'.

title: Swing and the big bands
description: In the swing era (about 1935 to the mid-1940s) big dance bands played sections of brass, woodwinds and rhythm off against each other, with a forward momentum called swing.

facts.text: The swing era ran from about 1935 to the mid-1940s, when big dance bands were at their most popular.
Swing bands grouped players into sections of brass, woodwinds and rhythm, played off against each other in musical dialogue.
Swing is a compelling momentum that comes from how musicians attack and accent notes against fixed beats.
Swing music went with African American social dances like the lindy hop.

title: Fletcher Henderson, Benny Goodman and the color line
description: Black bandleader Fletcher Henderson's arrangements shaped Benny Goodman's 'King of Swing' sound; Goodman's integrated small groups gave Black musicians visibility during segregation.

facts.text: Bands led by the Black pianist Fletcher Henderson in the 1920s were especially important in spreading the ideas of big-band swing.
Benny Goodman, billed as the 'King of Swing', got his band's most characteristic sound from Fletcher Henderson's arrangements.
Goodman hired pianist Teddy Wilson, though he feared the consequences, and Lionel Hampton in 1936, giving Black musicians visibility during segregation.

title: Duke Ellington writes for his players
description: Duke Ellington led his band for more than 50 years and wrote for the particular sounds of its members, as his 'Mood Indigo' score shows.

facts.text: Duke Ellington (1899-1974), born in Washington, D.C., led his band for more than half a century and composed thousands of scores.
Ellington composed works to highlight the special talents of his soloists.
Ellington's short score for 'Mood Indigo' (1930) names players, not instruments: 'Barney' for Barney Bigard, 'Tricky' for Joe 'Tricky Sam' Nanton.
'Mood Indigo' (1930) was set for muted trumpet, unmuted trombone and low-register clarinet.

title: The Cotton Club and segregation
description: Ellington's orchestra became the house band at Harlem's Cotton Club in 1927, a club that featured Black entertainers for a whites-only audience.

facts.text: Harlem's Cotton Club featured Black entertainers but limited its audience to white patrons; Ellington's orchestra became its house band in 1927.
In 1999 the Pulitzer board gave Ellington a posthumous special citation for musical genius that evoked the principles of democracy through jazz.

title: Bebop
description: Bebop took shape in early-1940s Harlem jam sessions: small groups, rapid tempos and solos built on the chords, made for listening rather than dancing.

facts.text: Bebop took shape in the early 1940s in jam sessions at Minton's Playhouse in Harlem.
Bebop's pioneers included saxophonist Charlie Parker, trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie, pianist Thelonious Monk and drummer Kenny Clarke.
Bebop grew out of and against the swing bands: small combos, extremely rapid tempos, and improvised lines based on the harmony rather than the melody.
Bebop shifted jazz from dance music toward music for listening, as ballroom dancing declined during World War II.
At first, bebop was unacceptable not only to the general public but also to many musicians.

title: Bebop's higher intervals
description: Charlie Parker built melodies from a chord's higher intervals (9th, 11th, 13th), and bebop players added substituted chords to older jazz harmony.

facts.text: Parker recalled being bored with the stereotyped chord changes of 1939: 'I kept thinking there's bound to be something else.'
Jamming on 'Cherokee' in December 1939, Parker began building melodies from a chord's higher intervals, like the 9th, 11th and 13th, beyond root, 3rd, 5th, 7th.
Bebop took the harmonies of older jazz and superimposed extra 'substituted' chords on them.

title: Improvising over the changes
description: Jazz soloists invent melodies on the spot over a tune's chord progression, turning a familiar tune into something personal; hard progressions like 'Cherokee' tested them.

facts.text: Improvisation is one of jazz's chief traits: in most jazz performances, players take solos they make up on the spot.
Jazz soloists invent melodies over a tune's chord progression, played by the rhythm section (piano, guitar, bass) with drums.
Jazz makes a familiar tune everyone knows into something fresh and personal.
Ray Noble's 'Cherokee' has a 64-measure form whose chord changes challenged many jazz improvisers from 1938 to 1945.
Parker's 'Ko Ko' (1945) uses the chord structure of 'Cherokee' with its theme left out; it joined the National Recording Registry in 2002.

title: Call-and-response in jazz
description: Jazz players often answer each other, one instrument, voice or section replying to another, the same shape as spirituals and work songs.

facts.text: You can often hear call-and-response in jazz, with one instrument, voice or part of the band answering another.

title: The Great Migration carries the music north
description: About six million Black Americans left the rural South between the 1910s and 1970, fleeing Jim Crow; the blues and jazz moved north with them, to Chicago and beyond.

facts.text: From the 1910s to 1970, about six million Black Americans moved from the rural South to cities in the North and West, like Chicago, Detroit and New York.
Migrants left Jim Crow laws and sharecropping for more jobs, though racism was rampant in the North too.
Great Migration migrants changed the sound of the blues they brought north with them.
A World War I boom in Chicago meant jobs for musicians, and New Orleans players, including cornetist Joe 'King' Oliver, went north.

title: The first recording nobody could play
description: Scott de Martinville's 1860 phonautograph drew sound on soot-covered paper but could not play it back; it was first heard in 2008.

facts.text: In 1860 Edouard-Leon Scott de Martinville recorded a singer performing Au Clair de la Lune with his phonautograph, which scratched sound waves onto soot-covered paper and was never meant to play them back.

In March 2008, 148 years after it was made, physicist Carl Haber of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory turned Scott's 1860 tracing into sound: the earliest recording of a human voice ever played back.

title: Edison's phonograph
description: Edison's 1877 tinfoil phonograph was the first machine to both record and play back sound, by pressing vibrations into foil and tracing them back out.

facts.text: Thomas Edison's phonograph of 1877 was the first machine to both record sound and play it back.
For his first test of the phonograph, Edison recorded the nursery rhyme Mary Had a Little Lamb.
In the tinfoil phonograph, sound shook a diaphragm and a needlelike stylus that pressed tiny pits into tinfoil wrapped around a cylinder, turned by a hand crank for both recording and playing.
For playback, a lighter stylus traced the pits in the foil, shaking a second diaphragm and re-creating the original sound.

title: Radio's national audience
description: Radio grew from KDKA's 1920 broadcast to 40.3 percent of US households by 1930, and networks like NBC sent one program to many cities at once.

facts.text: KDKA in Pittsburgh, recognized as the first commercial radio station in the United States, began broadcasting on November 2, 1920, with the Harding-Cox presidential election results.
The 1930 census found that 12,048,762 US households, 40.3 percent, owned a radio.
NBC, the first organized national radio network, made its first broadcast on November 15, 1926, from New York over 25 stations in 21 cities, reaching as far west as Kansas City.

title: Payola
description: Airplay was so valuable that record promoters secretly paid disc jockeys; the late-1950s payola scandal led Congress to amend the Communications Act in 1960.

facts.text: Payola is an undercover payment to a disc jockey or radio personality for promoting a record; in the late-1950s payola scandal, deejays took bribes to push records and many lost their jobs.
In 1960 Congress amended the Communications Act, largely because of the payola scandals, redefining when broadcasts must identify who paid for them.

title: Rock and roll's roots
description: Rock and roll arose in the mid-1950s US from rhythm and blues and country, with gospel influence; its first stars included Black artists, and Elvis Presley and Chuck Berry crossed the styles.

facts.text: Britannica describes rock and roll, which arose in the United States in the mid-1950s, as a merger of country music and rhythm and blues.
Early rock and roll stars Fats Domino, Little Richard, Chuck Berry and Bo Diddley were Black artists who only years before would have been called rhythm-and-blues artists.
Cleveland disc jockey Alan Freed played hard-driving rhythm-and-blues records that introduced white teenagers to the new sound.
Sister Rosetta Tharpe sang gospel songs to her own electric guitar and influenced Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis and Elvis Presley.
Chuck Berry's 1955 hit Maybellene was a country-influenced song he had first titled Ida Red.
In July 1954 at Sam Phillips' Sun Records, Elvis Presley recorded Arthur Crudup's blues song That's All Right, drawing on country, gospel and blues, and he was careful to credit his Black sources.

title: The first rock and roll record?
description: Rocket 88 (1951) is often billed as the first rock and roll record, but rock and roll grew gradually and has earlier contenders, such as Sister Rosetta Tharpe's 1944 recording.

facts.text: Rocket 88, recorded in March 1951 at Sam Phillips' Memphis studio by Ike Turner's Kings of Rhythm with singer Jackie Brenston, is often billed as the first rock and roll record.
The Library of Congress notes that rock and roll was the product of a gradual evolution, with earlier contenders for the first record.
Rocket 88's guitar had an accidental fuzzy tone; legend blames an amplifier damaged on the way to the session.
Some musicologists call a 1944 Sister Rosetta Tharpe recording the first rock-and-roll song, and she entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as an early influence in 2018.

title: How an electric guitar pickup works
description: A magnetic pickup turns a steel string's vibration into a voltage at the same frequency, which an amplifier makes loud through a speaker.

facts.text: As performance spaces grew, guitars were hard to hear over other instruments, especially horns.
The 1931 Frying Pan, built by George Beauchamp and Adolph Rickenbacker, became the first widely recognized electric guitar.
The Frying Pan's electromagnetic pickup used a pair of horseshoe magnets around the strings with a coil of wire underneath.
A magnetic pickup works by Faraday's law: a vibrating steel string changes the magnetic field through a coil, inducing a voltage that vibrates at the string's own frequency.
The pickup's electrical signal goes to an amplifier, which makes it louder and sends it out through a speaker; the sound can also be distorted and modified.

title: The solid-body electric guitar
description: Hollow electric guitars suffered distortion, overtones and feedback, so makers built solid bodies: Les Paul in the early 1940s, then Fender and Gibson by 1952.

facts.text: Early hollow-body electric guitars suffered from distortion, overtones and feedback, which pushed makers toward solid bodies.
Les Paul built a solid-body electric guitar in the early 1940s, and by 1952 Fender and Gibson were both selling solid-body models.

title: Beatlemania
description: The Beatles, from Liverpool and steeped in American rock and roll, reached 73 million US viewers on February 9, 1964, and held the Hot 100's top five on April 4, 1964.

facts.text: On February 9, 1964, 73 million people watched the Beatles' US television debut on The Ed Sullivan Show, more than 60 percent of US TV viewers that evening.
The Beatles were four young musicians from the seaport city of Liverpool, England.
The Beatles grew out of a shared love of American rock and roll; Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Fats Domino and Elvis Presley were among their inspirations.
On the Billboard Hot 100 dated April 4, 1964, the Beatles held all top five spots, with Can't Buy Me Love at No. 1.
John Lennon and Paul McCartney wrote the Beatles' original songs together as a songwriting partnership.

title: The studio as instrument
description: In 1966 the Beatles stopped performing live to concentrate on the studio; Sgt. Pepper (1967) took months at Abbey Road and ran its songs together.

facts.text: In 1966 the Beatles retired from performing live to concentrate on the recording studio.

Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967) took months at EMI's Abbey Road studios, unheard-of for pop; its songs run into each other without the usual pause, and George Martin called the studio a creative playground.

title: Motown, the hit factory
description: Berry Gordy founded Motown in Detroit in 1959 with an $800 family loan and ran it like an assembly line, with house writers, a house band and quality control.

facts.text: Berry Gordy Jr. founded Motown in Detroit in January 1959 with an $800 loan from his family.
Motown's two-story house on Detroit's West Grand Boulevard became its studio and headquarters, Hitsville.
Motown became one of the most successful Black-owned businesses in American history.

Gordy said a brief stint on an auto-plant assembly line taught him about making a quality product; Motown used in-house songwriters like Holland-Dozier-Holland, a house band called the Funk Brothers, and strict quality control.
Britannica credits Motown with the highest hit ratio for its released singles of any record company in history.
Motown records were mixed to sound good on car radios, and the label called itself the Sound of Young America.

title: Soul music
description: Soul, an African American style of the 1950s to 1970s, returned to gospel and blues roots; Aretha Franklin's Respect (1967) became an anthem for civil rights and women's equality.

facts.text: Soul music, an African American genre that grew from the 1950s into the 1970s, returned to gospel and blues roots, with church-style call and response and long melodic runs; Ray Charles helped start it by turning gospel songs secular.

Otis Redding wrote and first recorded Respect; Aretha Franklin, raised singing in the Baptist church, reworked it with a spelled-out R-E-S-P-E-C-T and sock it to me, and it topped the Hot 100 on June 3, 1967.
Respect became an anthem for civil rights and women's equality, though Franklin said she had recorded it as a male-female song.

title: Music festivals
description: Woodstock (1969) drew about 400,000 people to a farm in Bethel, New York, and ended with Hendrix's anthem; Live Aid (1985) linked stadiums on two continents.

facts.text: Woodstock took place on August 15-18, 1969, on Max Yasgur's farm in Bethel, New York, not in the town of Woodstock; the organizers kept the Woodstock name.
About 400,000 people came to Woodstock, most getting in without paying because security was thin, and rain turned the site to mud.
Woodstock nearly bankrupted its four inexperienced promoters; Michael Wadleigh's 1970 documentary film was a commercial success that recouped their losses.
Jimi Hendrix took the Woodstock stage around 9 a.m. on Monday, August 18, 1969, after many festivalgoers had already left.
In his Star-Spangled Banner, Hendrix used his electric guitar to sound like rockets and bombs bursting and a siren-like wail, an example of text painting.
Live Aid, on July 13, 1985, ran at the same time at Wembley Stadium in London and JFK Stadium in Philadelphia to raise money for famine relief in Ethiopia, and was broadcast worldwide.

title: Heavy metal and the power chord
description: The power chord is a root plus fifth, neither major nor minor and clear under distortion; heavy metal, codified in the 1970s, built on it.

facts.text: A power chord is two notes, a root and the fifth above it, often used in rock music.
With no third, a power chord is neither major nor minor.
Power chords are a staple of rock, punk and metal, and they stay clear under heavy distortion, where full chords get muddy.
In the mid-1960s, British bands Cream and the Yardbirds and guitarist Jimi Hendrix developed a heavier sound; in the 1970s Led Zeppelin, Deep Purple and Black Sabbath codified heavy metal.
Heavy metal is defined by amplified distortion, heavy riffs, power chords and a blues-based foundation.
The phrase heavy metal appeared in a 1968 Steppenwolf song before critics adopted it for the style in the early 1970s.

title: Punk
description: Punk came together in 1975-80 in New York and London (the Ramones, the Sex Pistols) with short, fast, minimal songs that rejected polished rock.

facts.text: Punk coalesced into an international movement between 1975 and 1980, emerging in New York and London at about the same time.
At New York's CBGB club, the Ramones' 1976 debut album became the blueprint for punk; in Britain, the Sex Pistols' 1977 hits made the country punk's epicenter.
Punk songs were short, fast and minimal, rejecting the polished production of earlier rock, and punk fueled independent record labels.

title: MTV and the music video
description: MTV (launched August 1, 1981) made image as important as sound; Michael Jackson's videos helped break racial barriers, and Thriller became the first music video in the National Film Registry.

facts.text: MTV launched just after midnight on August 1, 1981, with Video Killed the Radio Star by the Buggles.
MTV showed music videos continuously, introduced by video disc jockeys, or VJs.
MTV made visual presentation as important as the music in selling records.
MTV struggled at first; its fortunes changed when it added rhythm and blues artists, and Michael Jackson's videos for Billie Jean and Beat It showed that MTV exposure could make a star.
Britannica credits Beat It with helping break down the barriers between Black and white artists on radio and in music videos.
Michael Jackson's Thriller video (1983), directed by John Landis and about 14 minutes long, became in 2009 the first music video added to the National Film Registry.
By the mid-1990s, most of MTV's schedule was non-music programming such as reality shows, game shows and cartoons.

title: The National Recording Registry
description: Each year the Librarian of Congress adds 25 recordings at least 10 years old to the National Recording Registry; this chapter's milestones are on it.

facts.text: Under the National Recording Preservation Act of 2000, the Librarian of Congress adds 25 recordings each year to the National Recording Registry: culturally, historically or aesthetically significant, and at least 10 years old.
Scott de Martinville's phonautograms, including his 1860 Au Clair de la Lune, have been added to the National Recording Registry.
Rocket 88 (1951) was added to the National Recording Registry in 2024.
Elvis Presley's 1954-55 Sun recordings were added to the National Recording Registry in 2002.
Aretha Franklin's Respect (1967) was in the National Recording Registry's first class, in 2002.
The Beatles' Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967) was added to the National Recording Registry in 2003.

title: Hip-hop begins in the Bronx
description: Hip-hop is commonly dated to DJ Kool Herc's August 1973 party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx, and was built by the Bronx's Black and Latino youth, with Jamaican sound-system roots.

facts.text: On August 11, 1973, Cindy Campbell and her brother Clive (DJ Kool Herc) held a back-to-school party in the rec room of their building at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx, raising money for her school clothes.
Kool Herc's August 1973 Bronx party is the date most commonly cited for the birth of hip-hop, whose 50th anniversary was celebrated in 2023.
DJ Kool Herc was born in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1955 and moved to the Bronx in 1967; he was influenced by Kingston's dance-hall parties and the sound systems their deejays built.
Kool Herc owned the loudest sound system in his Bronx neighborhood and played soul and funk through a Kingston, Jamaica-style sound system.
In Jamaican toasting, the deejay spoke, or rapped, improvised rhymes over the music; the tradition influenced Kool Herc.
Hip-hop was born in the early-1970s Bronx, then hit hard by poverty, among Black and Latino youth drawing on African American, Afro-Caribbean and Afro-Latino traditions.

title: Hip-hop's four elements
description: Hip-hop is a culture of four core elements: DJing, MCing (rapping), breaking and graffiti; Herc named the break dancers b-boys and b-girls.

facts.text: Hip-hop culture has four core elements: DJing (turntable work), MCing (rapping), breaking (breakdancing) and graffiti.
Kool Herc called the dancers who performed during a record's percussive instrumental breaks break-boys and break-girls, or b-boys and b-girls.

title: The turntable as an instrument
description: Herc's merry-go-round looped a record's drum break with two copies on two turntables (the breakbeat); Grand Wizzard Theodore added scratching.

facts.text: Herc favored the percussive instrumental breaks of funk records, and noticed that the breaks brought the most people out to dance.
Herc's merry-go-round used two turntables, a mixer and two copies of the same record to loop and extend a song's break for dancers; today it is known as the breakbeat.
In 1975, in his Bronx bedroom, Theodore Livingston accidentally moved a record back and forth while reaching to pause it as his mother spoke, and liked the scratching sound.
Bronx DJ Grand Wizzard Theodore is credited with inventing scratching; a turntable he used is in the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture.

title: Sampling
description: Sampling builds new tracks from music and sounds extracted from other recordings; drum breaks such as Funky Drummer are favorite samples.

facts.text: Britannica defines digital sampling as music and sounds extracted from other recordings; rap's backing music, which can include it, is also called hip-hop.
Clyde Stubblefield's 20-second drum solo on James Brown's 1970 single Funky Drummer has been called the most sampled drum break in music.

title: Rap, rhyme and flow
description: Rap is rhythmic, rhyming speech over music; flow is the rhythm and articulation of the delivery. Early rap rhymed on beat four; later rap scattered rhymes and accents.

facts.text: Britannica defines rap as a style in which rhythmic and/or rhyming speech is chanted, or rapped, to musical accompaniment.
Music theorist Kyle Adams defines flow as all the rhythmic and articulative features of a rapper's delivery: where syllables and accents fall against the beat, and how they are articulated.
Analyses of early-1980s rap find rhymed line endings falling on or near the fourth beat of bar after bar.
Later rap placed rhymes and accents less predictably, with internal rhymes, offbeat rhymes and syncopation.

title: Rap reaches the charts
description: Rap grew in African American communities in New York City and reached national prominence with the Sugarhill Gang's Rapper's Delight (1979), now in the National Recording Registry.

facts.text: Britannica says rap originated in African American communities in New York City and came to national prominence with the Sugarhill Gang's Rapper's Delight (1979).
The Sugarhill Gang's Rapper's Delight (1979) reached No. 36 on the Billboard Hot 100 and was added to the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry in 2011.

title: How a synthesizer makes sound
description: A synthesizer builds sound electronically: an oscillator sets pitch, a filter removes harmonics to shape timbre (subtractive synthesis), and an envelope (ADSR) shapes loudness over time.

facts.text: A synthesizer produces sounds electronically; analog synthesis manipulates electrical currents to generate sounds.
On the Moog synthesizer, the keyboard set the pitch by sending the oscillator a voltage that depended on which key was pressed.
A sawtooth wave contains all the harmonics of its fundamental pitch, which makes it a rich starting point for filtering.
In subtractive synthesis, filters remove part of a harmonically rich wave to control its harmonic content, shaping timbre while the oscillator sets the pitch.

A synthesizer envelope shapes loudness in four stages: attack (the rise when a key is pressed), decay (the fall to a steady level), sustain (held while the key is down) and release (the fade after it is let go).

title: The Moog synthesizer
description: Robert Moog unveiled his modular synthesizer in 1964; Switched-On Bach (1968) made it famous, and the portable Minimoog followed in 1970.

facts.text: In October 1964 Robert Moog unveiled his Moog Modular System, the first complete voltage-controlled modular synthesizer, at the Audio Engineering Society convention.
Wendy Carlos's 1968 album Switched-On Bach, Bach played on a Moog synthesizer, brought the synthesizer into the spotlight.
Moog introduced the small, portable Minimoog in 1970.

title: From disco to house
description: Disco grew in early-1970s New York clubs on a four-on-the-floor kick; house grew from it in Chicago, named after Frankie Knuckles's Warehouse club.

facts.text: Disco faced a fierce backlash, notably at Disco Demolition Night in Chicago in 1979.
Disco began in underground clubs in the early 1970s, particularly in New York City, serving largely Black, Latino and LGBTQ+ communities; DJs used 12-inch singles to build extended mixes.
A four-on-the-floor beat puts the bass drum on every one of the four beats in each bar; it became central to 1970s disco and to house.

Frankie Knuckles was resident DJ from 1977 at the Warehouse, a members-only Chicago club for Black gay dancers; he re-edited disco records on reel-to-reel tape, and house music was named after the club.
House, born in Chicago clubs in the early 1980s, fused disco's soul vocals and four-to-the-floor kick with synthesizer sounds, and reached Europe by 1986.

title: Detroit techno
description: Techno came from young African American DJ-producers in Detroit in the mid-1980s: mostly instrumental, with synth melodies and more complex machine beats than house.

facts.text: Techno grew from middle-class African American youths in Detroit; Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson began drawing attention in 1985, influenced partly by Kraftwerk.
Detroit techno had glacial synthesizer melodies and brisk machine rhythms, was mostly instrumental, and used more complex beats than house's four-to-the-floor kick.

title: Reggae and the offbeat
description: Reggae came from Jamaica in the late 1960s, after ska and rocksteady; its groove sets short guitar or keyboard chords on the offbeats. UNESCO listed it as heritage in 2018.

facts.text: In 2018 UNESCO inscribed the reggae music of Jamaica on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Reggae originated in Jamaica in the late 1960s, emerging from marginalized communities in western Kingston.
Reggae grew out of earlier Jamaican styles: ska developed into rocksteady, which developed into reggae.
Reggae uses a heavy four-beat rhythm of drums and bass, while the rhythm guitar or keyboard plays short, choppy chords on the offbeats.
Reggae influenced later styles, including dancehall and hip-hop.

title: Bob Marley
description: Bob Marley and the Wailers carried reggae and its social message worldwide from the 1970s; at the 1978 One Love Peace Concert he joined rival leaders' hands.

facts.text: Bob Marley, born in 1945 in Nine Miles, Jamaica, formed the Wailers in Trench Town with Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer; they wrote songs for and about poor West Indians.
Reggae's lyrics grew increasingly political, addressing social and economic injustice, and it became associated with the Rastafari movement through Bob Marley and the Wailers.
After the Wailers signed with Island Records in 1972, their album Catch a Fire brought reggae to audiences worldwide.
Bob Marley died of cancer in 1981, aged 36.
At the 1978 One Love Peace Concert in Kingston, held amid political violence, Marley brought rival leaders Michael Manley and Edward Seaga onstage and held their joined hands aloft.

title: K-pop goes global
description: BTS topped the Billboard 200 in 2018 with an album sung mostly in Korean, the first K-pop act to do so, before their first English-language song.

facts.text: In 2018, BTS's album Love Yourself: Tear reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200, the first time a K-pop act topped the chart; most BTS songs are sung in Korean.
Producer Bang Si-Hyuk's Big Hit Entertainment began assembling BTS in 2010; their songs, mostly in Korean, focus on self-love, individuality and empowerment.
BTS's first English-language song, Dynamite (2020), debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.

title: Afrobeats
description: Afrobeats is 2000s West African pop from Nigeria and Ghana, distinct from Fela Kuti's political Afrobeat; it reached global charts in the 2010s.

facts.text: Afrobeats is a West African style that emerged in Nigeria and Ghana in the early 2000s, fusing highlife, dancehall and soca, with upbeat lyrics about love, success and partying.
Afrobeats differs from Fela Kuti's Afrobeat of the 1960s and 70s, which blended Yoruba music with jazz and funk and addressed political issues.
Drake's 2016 song One Dance, featuring Wizkid, topped the Billboard Hot 100 for 10 weeks.
Nigerian artist Burna Boy won the Grammy for Best Global Music Album in 2021 for Twice as Tall, his first Grammy.

title: Latin pop and Despacito
description: Despacito led the Billboard Hot 100 for 16 weeks in 2017, the longest No. 1 run for a mainly non-English song.

facts.text: Billboard reported that the Spanish-language Despacito, by Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee (remix featuring Justin Bieber), led the Hot 100 for 16 weeks in 2017, tying the record then, the longest No. 1 run for a mainly non-English song.

title: Auto-Tune
description: Auto-Tune detects a note's pitch and moves it to the nearest semitone; used subtly it corrects, pushed hard it makes the robotic 'Believe' effect.

facts.text: Cher's 1998 hit Believe was the first commercial recording to intentionally feature the audible side effects of Auto-Tune.
Andy Hildebrand interpreted seismic data for the oil industry from 1976 to 1989; his company, Antares Audio Technologies, released Auto-Tune in the late 1990s.
Auto-Tune detects the pitch of a sung note and moves it to the nearest true semitone, tuning the vocal.
Pushed hard, Auto-Tune makes a voice leap from note to note while staying unnaturally in tune; subtle correction and this overt effect are both now widely used.

title: Reverb in the studio
description: Reverb is sound lingering after its source stops; studios record dry and add artificial reverb, and a drier sound seems closer.

facts.text: Reverberation is the persistence of sound after its source has stopped, built from many reflections within a space.
Studios are often made acoustically dry with absorbent material, and reverb is added artificially with plates, springs or digital algorithms; the stronger the dry sound, the closer it seems.

title: Digital sound and the CD
description: The CD (1982) stores sound as numbers, sampling 44,100 times a second, a little over twice the roughly 20 kHz top of human hearing.

facts.text: The compact disc, co-invented by Philips and Sony, went on sale in 1982; it stores sound as digital data in microscopic pits and flat lands read by a laser.
CD audio is sampled 44,100 times a second; sampling must exceed twice the highest frequency, about 20 kHz, so the rate must be above about 40,000 per second.

title: MP3 compression
description: MP3, from Fraunhofer IIS, stores sounds the ear can't perceive with less precision, making files up to ten times smaller; Napster spread shared files in 1999.

facts.text: Fraunhofer IIS researchers developed MP3, which stores sound components the ear can't perceive with less precision, making files up to ten times smaller with virtually no audible difference.
The .mp3 file extension was chosen on July 14, 1995, through an internal email poll at Fraunhofer IIS.
Napster, created in 1999 by college student Shawn Fanning, let people share music files over the internet; it shut down in 2001 after the RIAA won a court injunction.

title: Streaming takes over
description: Streaming services such as Spotify (2008) replaced owning music; the RIAA reported streaming at 82% of US recorded-music revenue in 2025.

facts.text: The RIAA reported that streaming made up 82% of US recorded-music revenue in 2025, measured at wholesale.
Spotify, founded in Sweden in 2006, launched in 2008 and streams music instead of selling files, with a free ad-supported tier and paid subscriptions.

title: The TR-808 drum machine
description: Roland's TR-808 (1980) synthesized its drum sounds from circuits; dismissed as fake and discontinued, it became central to hip-hop through records like Planet Rock.

facts.text: Roland's TR-808 drum machine came out in 1980; critics said it didn't sound like real drums, and Roland stopped making it after about 12,000 were sold.
Roland's engineers used analog synthesis, manipulating electrical currents, to make the 808's imitation hand-claps and bass notes; its thundering bass became famous.
Planet Rock (1982), made with an 808 by Afrika Bambaataa and the Soul Sonic Force, reached No. 48 on the Billboard charts and became one of the decade's most influential records.

title: From ear to brain
description: Hair cells turn sound vibrations into electrical signals that the auditory nerve carries to the brain; an area at the top of each temporal lobe receives information from the ears.

facts.text: Hair cells in the cochlea turn vibrations into an electrical signal; the auditory nerve carries it to the brain, which turns it into a sound we recognize.
An area at the top of each temporal lobe of the brain receives information from the ears.

title: The beat reaches movement areas
description: Listening to a regular beat engages movement-related brain areas even when the listener is still.

facts.text: In a 2007 brain-imaging study, rhythms with a regular beat drove more activity in movement areas (basal ganglia, supplementary motor area), with listeners not moving.

title: Music and the reward chemical
description: Pleasurable music that gives chills releases dopamine in the striatum, in one part while anticipating the peak and another at the peak itself.

facts.text: A 2011 brain-imaging study found dopamine released in the striatum at peak moments of pleasurable music that gave listeners chills.
In the same study, dopamine release in the caudate was tied to anticipating the peak, and in the nucleus accumbens to the peak itself.
Dopamine is also involved in the pleasure of tangible rewards such as food.

title: The Mozart effect myth
description: The 1993 Mozart effect was a brief spatial-task boost; a 2010 meta-analysis found little evidence of any specific Mozart effect.

facts.text: A 1993 study reported students did better on a spatial-reasoning task after a Mozart sonata, but the boost lasted no more than about 15 minutes.
A 2010 meta-analysis of nearly 40 studies found little evidence of a specific Mozart effect; other music gave similar small effects.

title: Earworms are common
description: Earworms (involuntary musical imagery) are reported weekly by about 9 in 10 people and are usually short snippets of a tune.

facts.text: In a survey of over 12,000 Finnish internet users, about 9 in 10 reported an earworm (involuntary musical imagery) at least once a week.
Most earworms are short snippets of a larger tune, not the whole song.

title: What makes a song sticky
description: Earworm songs tend to be faster, with common melodic contours and an unusual interval or repetition.

facts.text: A 2016 study of 3,000 people found earworms were faster than similarly popular songs, with common melodic shapes plus unusual leaps or repetitions.
The songs most often named as earworms were Bad Romance (Lady Gaga), Don't Stop Believin' (Journey) and Can't Get You Out of My Head (Kylie Minogue).

title: Evicting an earworm
description: Seeking out the tune and distraction are common, effective responses; chewing gum reduced earworms in a 2015 study.

facts.text: In a 2014 study, the most popular and effective responses to earworms were listening to the tune itself and musical or verbal distraction.
A 2015 University of Reading study found chewing gum reduced earworms, likely by busying the mouth-movement planning used to sing a tune silently.

title: Music borrows the voice's emotional code
description: Voices and music express emotion with similar cues: sadness slow, soft and low; happiness fast, loud and high.

facts.text: A 2003 review of 104 voice and 41 music studies found emotion uses similar cues in both: sadness slow, soft and low; happiness fast, loud and high.

title: Why sad music can feel good
description: Music-evoked sadness is enjoyed when it is non-threatening, aesthetically pleasing and brings benefits such as mood regulation.

facts.text: A 2015 review found sad music enjoyable when it feels non-threatening, is aesthetically pleasing and brings benefits such as mood regulation.
The review notes that in art, the real-life circumstances that normally come with sadness, such as an actual loss, are absent.

title: Musical anhedonia
description: Some healthy people with normal music perception get little pleasure from music, yet respond normally to other rewards such as money.

facts.text: A 2014 study described healthy people with normal music perception who got little pleasure from music, yet responded normally to winning money.

title: Silent films had live music
description: Silent films were accompanied by live music from pianists, organists or, in big cities, orchestras.

facts.text: Silent films were usually accompanied live by a pianist, a theater organist or, in large cities, an orchestra.

title: The Jaws motif
description: John Williams's Jaws theme alternates two neighboring notes, E and F, growing louder and faster as the shark nears; it stands in for a shark seldom seen.

facts.text: John Williams built the shark theme for Jaws (1975) from two alternating notes, E and F.
The two-note Jaws motif grows louder and faster as the shark closes in.
The mechanical sharks kept failing, so the shark does not appear until the 81st minute of Jaws; the theme signals it instead.
John Williams won an Academy Award for the Jaws score.

title: Music changes what a scene means
description: In a 2001 study, the same ambiguous film clips were read more positively with positive music and more negatively with negative music, and memories shifted the same way.

facts.text: In a 2001 study, viewers read ambiguous film clips more positively with positive music, more negatively with negative music, and fairly neutrally with none.
A week later, viewers' memories of the clips were also biased in the direction of the music's mood.

title: Composing for a sound chip
description: Koji Kondo wrote Super Mario Bros. music for NES sound that offered three musical notes at a time plus one white-noise sound, with very little data.

facts.text: Koji Kondo said the NES sound he used for Super Mario Bros. offered just three musical notes at once plus one white-noise sound, with very little data.

title: Music that reacts to play
description: Game music can react to play: Kondo wrote Game Over jingles, goal fanfares and pieces that speed up as time runs short.

facts.text: Kondo wrote interactive music for Super Mario Bros.: jingles after Game Over, fanfares for reaching goals, pieces that sped up when time ran short.

title: Game music gains recognition
description: The Super Mario Bros. theme became the first video game music in the National Recording Registry (2023), and the Grammys first awarded a video game score prize in 2023.

facts.text: In 2023 the Super Mario Bros. theme (Koji Kondo, 1985) became the first video game music added to the Library of Congress National Recording Registry.
Kondo's Super Mario Bros. music has been performed by orchestras around the globe.
The first Grammy for Best Score Soundtrack for Video Games (2023) went to Stephanie Economou for Assassin's Creed Valhalla: Dawn of Ragnarok.

title: A song holds two copyrights
description: A recorded song involves two copyrights: the musical work (notes and lyrics, by songwriters) and the sound recording (by performers and producers).

facts.text: A recorded song involves two copyrights: the musical work (notes and lyrics, by songwriters) and the sound recording (by performers and producers).
Warner/Chappell collected licensing fees for Happy Birthday to You until a federal judge ruled in 2015 it held no valid copyright to the lyrics.

title: The US radio gap
description: In the US, the sound recording's performance right covers only digital transmissions, so AM/FM radio pays the musical work's owners (via PROs like ASCAP and BMI) but not the recording's.

facts.text: A musical work's copyright covers public performance, such as radio play; songwriters usually license it through organizations like ASCAP and BMI.
In the US, the performance right for sound recordings covers only digital transmissions, so AM/FM radio pays no royalties for the recording itself.

title: The mechanical royalty
description: For 2026 the US statutory mechanical royalty for a CD, vinyl or download copy of a song is 13.1 cents (or 2.52 cents per minute, whichever is larger).

facts.text: For 2026, the US statutory royalty for each song on a CD, vinyl record or download is 13.1 cents, or 2.52 cents a minute if that is larger.

title: Deliberate practice
description: In a 1993 Berlin study, the best student violinists reported the most solitary practice; Ericsson called focused, feedback-rich improvement work deliberate practice.

facts.text: A 1993 study grouped Berlin music-academy violin students as best, good or future music teachers, and asked each to estimate their past practice.
The best group reported about 7,400 hours of practice alone by age 18; the future music teachers about 3,400.
Deliberate practice is effortful work aimed at improving: well-defined tasks at the right difficulty, with informative feedback, unlike play.

title: What practice explains
description: Practice matters but explains only part of the differences between musicians: about 21% in a 2014 meta-analysis; a 2019 Berlin-style replication found best and good violinists did not differ significantly.

facts.text: A 2014 meta-analysis found deliberate practice explained about 21% of the differences in music performance.
A 2019 repeat of the Berlin violin study found no significant practice difference between the best and good violinists.

title: Absolute pitch is rare
description: Absolute (perfect) pitch is naming or producing a note with no reference; it is estimated at under 1 in 10,000 in the US and Europe and does not guarantee better musicianship.

facts.text: Absolute pitch (perfect pitch) is the ability to name or produce a note without hearing a reference note.
In the US and Europe, absolute pitch is estimated at fewer than 1 in 10,000 people.
Absolute pitch does not necessarily come with better performance on other musical tasks.
Most people without absolute pitch still have surprisingly accurate long-term memory for pitch when they needn't name the note.

title: Perfect pitch and tone languages
description: Absolute pitch is more common with earlier music training and far more common among Mandarin-speaking conservatory students, whose language uses pitch for meaning.

facts.text: A 2006 study of conservatory students found more absolute pitch with earlier training, and far more among Mandarin speakers in Beijing than US students.
In Mandarin, a tone language, pitch changes meaning: ma can mean mother, hemp, horse or a reproach, depending on the tone.

title: Copland's three planes of listening
description: In What to Listen for in Music (1939), Aaron Copland described listening on sensuous, expressive and sheerly musical planes, and urged active listening for something.

facts.text: American composer Aaron Copland wrote What to Listen for in Music, published in 1939.
Copland described three planes of listening: sensuous (the pleasure of the sound), expressive (feeling) and sheerly musical (the notes themselves).
Copland wrote that casual listeners notice melody first, then rhythm, and take harmony and tone color for granted.
Copland said we really listen on all three planes at once, and urged being someone who is listening for something.

title: Safe listening
description: WHO: 80 dB is safe for up to 40 hours a week and 90 dB for only 4; keep devices at or under 60% volume. Human hair cells do not grow back, but noise-induced hearing loss is preventable.

facts.text: WHO says 80 dB is safe for up to 40 hours a week, but at 90 dB safe listening time drops to four hours a week.
WHO advises keeping a personal audio device at no more than 60% of its maximum volume.
Human hair cells in the inner ear do not grow back once destroyed, but noise-induced hearing loss is completely preventable.
